## Databricks Building Blocks

### How Databricks Fits Together – Lesson 1

Hello, dear friends. In this lesson, we are starting a brand new section. Yes, in the very first lesson of this new section, we'll talk about the architecture of Databricks. That is, how its infrastructure works. When we say architecture, what we really mean is this. What components are behind the system, where are they located, and how do they communicate with each other? You can think of it like the layout of a city. In a city, roads, buildings, power lines, and water systems all work together in harmony. Databricks also has such an infrastructure plan. Friends, the architecture of Databricks consists of two main parts, the control plane and the compute plane. The control plane is like the brain of Databricks. The user interface you see when logging in through your browser, cluster management, security and access controls such as Unity Catalog, all of these run here. Small but important details like previous versions of your notebooks or job history are also stored here. In other words, you can think of the control plane as the system's management center. On the other side, we have the compute plane. This is the muscle of Databricks. Actual data processing, Spark jobs, and SQL queries all take place here. For example, suppose you have a large Excel table. When you want to perform filtering or aggregation, the compute plane does that work. Now we can examine the compute plane under two categories, classic compute and serverless compute. So what is classic compute? In this model, the machines are launched inside your own cloud account. If you're using Azure, the machines run in your Azure subscription within a dedicated resource group. If you're on AWS, the machines are launched in your AWS account as EC2 instances. If you're on GCP, the machines live inside your Google project. You can think of this like owning your own car. The car's in your garage, you drive it, and all costs are your responsibility. Serverless compute, on the other hand, works differently. Here, the machines are not in your account. They are hosted in Databricks' own subscription. When you request a cluster, Databricks quickly assigns you a machine from this pool. This is like taking a taxi. The vehicle is ready, you call it, use it for your job, and then it goes back. You don't deal with maintenance or setup. The main advantage is that it starts up very quickly. When working in Databricks, you decide whether to use classic or serverless compute. When creating a new cluster or SQL warehouse, you specify which compute type you want. If you choose classic compute, the machines are launched in your cloud subscription. You have control. You can choose the machine size configuration and make custom adjustments. If you choose serverless compute, the machines are already waiting in Databricks' subscription. This model starts much faster, and you don't deal with infrastructure management. It's especially ideal for short tasks and ad hoc queries. For those using community edition, there is no such choice. Databricks automatically provides a serverless-like environment in the background, and you can start using it directly. Now, let's move on to the storage part. When you create a workspace in Databricks, a storage area is automatically set up as well. This is where system data such as notebook histories, job records, and Spark logs are stored. You can also save your temporary data here. You can think of storage as the cities archive room or warehouse. All documents, records, and data are kept here in an organized way. In summary, control plane is the management center, like the brain. Compute plane is the muscle, the factory that does the work. Classic equals your own car, runs in your cloud account. Serverless equals a taxi. Machines are ready in Databricks' count. Storage is the archive room where data is stored. Yes, I explained the topic using metaphors. I'll end the lesson here. In the next lesson, we'll examine this topic practically on the platform. See you soon. Take care.

### Databricks Compute Options – Lesson 1

Dear friends, hello and welcome. In the previous lessons, if you remember, we talked about the architecture of Databricks. Specifically, the relationship between the control plane and the compute plane. In that lesson, we saw the big picture. The user interface and management tasks were in the control plane, while the actual computations were carried out in the compute plane. We also briefly introduced the options within the compute plane, such as classic compute and serverless compute. In other words, in the architecture lesson, we explained where the work happens. In this lesson, however, we are narrowing our focus. We'll only talk about compute. We will go into detail about which types of compute options exist in Databricks, what purposes they serve, and most importantly, which one we should choose in different scenarios. So, to summarize. In the architecture lesson, we answered the question, where? While in this lesson, we will answer the question, which one? First, let's recall the concept of compute. Compute essentially means a cluster. A cluster is made up of virtual machines. A machine called the driver node plans the jobs while the worker nodes execute them. That's why you might hear the terms compute and cluster used interchangeably. They both mean the same thing. In Databricks, we can think of compute options under two main categories, classic compute and serverless compute. Let's review them again, since this is important enough to appear in an exam. Classic compute is a model that runs entirely within your own cloud account. If you are using Azure, the machines are launched in your Azure subscription. If you are on AWS, they are launched in your AWS account. This model gives you full control. You decide which machine sides to use, which runtime version to run, and which libraries to install. However, startup time can be long, and as long as the cluster is running, it generates costs. Serverless compute, on the other hand, is fully managed by Databricks. When you request a cluster, the machines are ready within seconds. Thanks to auto scaling, they automatically grow or shrink based on your workload, and you don't need to manage anything. This option is especially useful for quick starts, short analyses, or running SQL queries through BI tools. Now let's dive a little deeper. Within classic compute, there are two types. Let's explain this with a real life example. Imagine you're cooking in your kitchen at home. The stove is always on, the pot is sitting there, and you can start cooking whenever you want. This is similar to an all-purpose cluster. While you are coding, cleaning data, or experimenting with new libraries, it's always ready. But keep in mind, the stove keeps burning until you turn it off. In other words, it constantly consumes energy, which translates into cost. The all-purpose cluster works the same way. It keeps running until you shut it down, continuously generating costs. Now let's also think about the job cluster. This time, let's use a restaurant analogy. When you place an order at a restaurant, the kitchen starts working, your meal is prepared, and served to you. Once the job is done, the kitchen closes, and the lights go off. That's exactly how a job cluster works. For example, if you have an ETL job that runs every night at 2 a.m., the cluster starts when the job begins, does its work, and shuts down immediately after finishing. Since it doesn't stay idle, the cost is much lower. However, if you want to use it again, the same cluster won't come back. A new job will spin up a new cluster. Now that we understand the cluster types, let's move on to some important features. Friends, there is a feature called pools. Think of it like a parking lot, where a few cars are always running with their engines warmed up. Normally, it takes a few minutes to get your own car out of the garage and warm it up, but the cars in the pool are ready. You just hop in and drive. In Databricks, pools work the same way. Clusters are pre-warmed, and startup time is greatly reduced. This provides both time and cost advantages, especially for teams that frequently start and stop clusters. Now let's talk about another compute option, SQL Warehouse. Think of this like a library. Inside, there are only books, and your only task is to read. You can't cook complex meals or repair engines here. You only read. SQL Warehouse is fully optimized for SQL workloads. It is ideal for connecting tools like Power BI or Hublow. It runs SQL queries very fast, but you cannot use it to run Spark code. So when should we use all these options? If you say, I wanna start quickly, I don't wanna wait, then serverless compute is the right choice for you. If you say, I write code, I need to install custom libraries, and I need an environment that is always on, then the all-purpose cluster is your friend. If you say, my job runs at certain times on a regular schedule and then shuts down, then the job cluster is ideal for you. If you say, I only write SQL, I generate reports, I'm an analyst, then SQL Warehouse is just right for you. And finally, if you say, I have to use a classic cluster, but the startup time is too long, that's where pools come in. As you can see in the architecture lesson, we previously drew the big picture, where the control plane is, where the compute is, where the storage is. Now with this lesson, we have gone deeper into the compute options. You've learned which compute type should be preferred in which scenario. From now on, when choosing a cluster in Databricks, there will be no question marks in your mind. All right, that's the end of this lesson. In the next lesson, we'll do some practice. See you there. Goodbye for now. Here's the English translation of your text, keeping the teaching style and clarity intact.

### Databricks Cluster Settings: Theoretical Guide and Certification Preparation

Hello dear friends. In this lesson we will talk about Databricks cluster configuration settings. First we need to understand this the free edition version we are currently using does not give us the chance to see all these settings in practice. But this is not something discouraging because in the Databricks certification exam and in real projects the real question you will face is which setting should I choose and when. In other words you are not expected to play with every part hands-on but you do need to know what each part does. That's why we will cover this lesson entirely in theory and this knowledge will be more than enough for the exam. Some of you might ask what exactly is a cluster? Let's clarify this concept first. Compute and cluster actually mean the same thing but we use different words depending on the context. When we say compute we refer generally to computing power, meaning the virtual machines running in the background. When we say cluster we emphasize how that computing power is organized. Think of it like this. Compute equals the engine itself, its power, horsepower. Cluster equals the type of vehicle carrying that engine, how many seats it has, and how the driver and passengers are arranged. That's why Databricks uses these terms interchangeably because when you create a compute environment you are essentially creating a cluster. But when we say cluster configuration Databricks allows you to adjust the detailed settings of the compute. Now that we've separated the compute and cluster concepts let's move on to how we can configure this cluster. So imagine we have a vehicle with its engine running. Do we want to make it a single seater car or turn it into a bus? Who will we put inside? Which engine will we choose? And how long do we want it to run? Cluster configuration gives us the ability to answer all these questions. First setting we will look at is whether it will be single node or multi-node. This is one of the fundamental settings that determines the capacity of the compute and which workloads it is suitable for. Here you can think of a node as a worker. In a single node cluster there is only one worker and this worker is both the foreman and the laborer. That means it both gives the orders and does the work itself. This is sufficient for small and simple tasks. For example a small data analysis or a quick prototype project is ideal. A multi-node cluster on the other hand consists of one foreman, driver, and many workers under them. The foreman distributes the tasks, each worker does their own part, and the job finishes much faster. That's why multi-node clusters are necessary for large ETL processes or large-scale data processing scenarios. Think of it like this. One painter may be enough to paint a small apartment, but to paint a stadium you need dozens of workers. Now let's look at access mode. The next setting is access modes. Here Databricks offers us three options, single user, shared access, and no isolation share. Single user. In this mode the cluster can only be used by one person. Think of it like your personal computer. Nobody else is on it and you have all the permissions. It supports all languages, Python, SQL, Scala, R, and is completely suitable for personal tasks. Shared access. This mode is similar to a shared office space. Multiple users can work on the same cluster, but everyone has their own desk, files, and cabinet. In other words, tasks don't get mixed up and there is security. This mode is especially preferred in corporate environments. It requires a premium workspace and supports Python, SQL, and in some cases Scala. No isolation shared. This, however, is a bit more risky. Shared environment. Think of it like an office where desks aren't separated. One person's files may mix with another's. There is no isolation, meaning if one user consumes too many resources it can disrupt the work of others. It is usable in many cases, but it is not recommended for production environments. Now let's move on to Databricks Runtime. You can think of this as the engine of the vehicle. Databricks Runtime is an optimized version of Spark along with bundled libraries. If you're only doing general data processing, the standard runtime is sufficient. But if you are working on machine learning, you would choose Databricks Runtime ML. This is like adding extra turbo parts to your engine. Libraries like TensorFlow, PyTorch, Keras, and XGBoost come pre-installed. There is also a special accelerator option here called Photon. Enabling Photon is like adding a turbocharger to your engine. Spark queries run much faster. This makes a significant difference, especially in big data workloads. Now we come to an important cost patrol feature, auto termination. Let's say you start a cluster and finish your work but forget to shut it down. In this case, the cluster stays on unnecessarily and adds to your bill. With auto termination, if a cluster is unused for a set period, it shuts down automatically. It's like having a smart system that turns off the lights for you if you forget to switch them off when leaving the house. The default time is 120 minutes, but you can set it to anything from 10 minutes to one day. This feature is critical for protecting both your personal budget and the company's budget in corporate projects. So dear friends, I believe the topic is now clearly understood. As I mentioned at the beginning of the lesson, since the free edition gives us a ready-to-use compute environment, we cannot adjust these settings ourselves. However, since they can appear in the certification exam, we have reviewed them theoretically. In short, you may have seen the create compute screen in some cases. In the free edition we're using, this is not available because only serverless warehouse is provided. But if we had a paid Databricks workspace, from that screen we would be able to create either an all-purpose cluster or a job cluster. For the certification exam, just knowing this screen is enough. For now, we don't have the option to demonstrate it in practice. Friends, I'll end the lesson here. See you in the next class.

## Lakehouse Architecture Fundamentals

### What is Lakehouse? – The Unified Data Platform

Dear friends, hello everyone. In this lesson, we will greet a new section. And in the very first class of this section, we will meet one of the most talked about concepts in the data world, the lakehouse. Friends, today we will learn about lakehouse architecture, one of the most important modern data approaches. To understand this concept, we first need to look back at the data management methods used in the past, along with their strengths and limitation, because the lakehouse emerged as a solution that combines these methods. It's not a standalone option that just appeared out of nowhere. That's why we'll proceed chronologically. Friends, it all started with a data warehouse. Since the 1980s, companies have been storing their data in data warehouses. These systems were especially suitable for structured data, that is, data organized into tables, rows, and columns. The advantage was clear. The data was very well organized, reports ran fast, and business analysts could easily access the information they needed to make decisions. To make it more concrete, think of a data warehouse as an official archive building. Documents are placed in folders, stored neatly on shelves, everything is highly organized. But this archive only accepts standard file formats. If a document comes in a different format, it won't be stored inside. Of course, as technology advanced, the variety of data naturally increased. In the 1980s, with the technology of the time, data was fairly uniform and simple. But as the years went on, data became more diverse, and naturally, the way we stored it had to evolve as well. This is where the well-known 3VS problem emerged. Volume, velocity, and variety. Volume, the amount of data, exploded. Social media, sensors, IoT. Velocity, the speed of data flow increased dramatically. Real-time data, logs, streaming. Variety, the diversity of data grew. Tables, JSON, images, videos, plus logs. Since data warehouses could only handle structured, row-and-column-based data, they could not cope with the complexity brought by the 3VS. Billions of rows of massive data, real-time streaming logs, and semi-structured or unstructured formats such as JSON, images, and videos became a huge challenge for traditional systems. As a solution to these problems, in the 2000s, the concept of the data lake emerged. Data lakes could store all types of data, structured, semi-structured, and even unstructured, for example, JSON, log files, images, videos. And thanks to cloud storage solutions, they were cheap and highly scalable. For data scientists, this was extremely valuable because they could directly access raw data. But there was one problem. When analysts tried to prepare reports from this lake, they ran into performance issues. In other words, for BI, business intelligence, reporting, a data lake was not strong enough. Let's break this down. The data scientist's job, building machine learning models, making predictions, running experimental analyses. For them, the type and richness of data matters most. A data lake could store JSON, CSV, images, videos, log files, anything. The data scientist could process this data with Python or R and run their own algorithms. Performance was not as critical since model training could take a long time anyway and leverage CPU-slash-GPU power. The key was having access to diverse and accurate data. The data analyst's job, reports, dashboards, quick visualizations with BI tools. When a business analyst or manager asks in the morning meeting, show me the sales trend from the last three months, the analyst needs to produce a chart within minutes. But in a data lake, the data is raw and unorganized. Running a query can be slow because the data isn't stored in optimized formats. Meanwhile, in a data warehouse, the data was stored in optimized tables with indexes. Queries could run at light speed. But companies need to do both machine learning and business intelligence. That's why the lakehouse was born, to meet the needs of both sides within a single structure. The lakehouse became the common ground that unites the two. A lakehouse is a new architecture that combines the organization and performance of a data warehouse with the flexibility and cost-effectiveness of a data lake. This means you can store both structured and unstructured data in the same environment and from the same platform, perform both reporting and machine learning tasks. What the lakehouse provides. Thanks to the lakehouse architecture, companies no longer need to store their data in two separate places. In the past, data had to be copied from a data lake into a data warehouse, which meant both time loss and added cost. With the lakehouse, however, both business intelligence reporting and AI-slash-machine learning workloads are supported on a single platform. It also ensures data reliability through ACID transactions, meaning the data stays consistent. Yes, we will cover what ACID means in more detail later. In summary, today's data is not only large, but also diverse and fast-moving. The lakehouse addresses all three of these challenges at once. On a single platform, you can store raw data, perform structured data analysis, and provide a powerful environment for data scientists. Executives make decisions with confidence, and data scientists build models with trustworthy data. The lakehouse is the unified platform of modern data management. It combines the performance and structure of the data warehouse with the flexibility and cost advantage of the data lake. That concludes this lesson. In the next class, we'll learn about the internal structure of the lakehouse, known as the medallion architecture, bronze-silver-gold model. See you in the next lesson. Goodbye for now.

----------------------------------------

### Understanding the Medallion Layers (Bronze, Silver, Gold)

Understanding the Medallion Layers, Bronze, Silver, Gold Layers Dear friends, hello everyone. As you know, in the previous lesson, I explained the lake house concept along with its history. Now we already understand what it is. One of the strongest aspects of the lake house architecture is that it can manage data in well-structured layers. This approach is called the medallion architecture. In this lesson, we will examine this approach in detail. Friends, the word medallion here is not a coincidence. It symbolizes how data gains value as it passes through each layer. Raw data, bronze is ingested, quality is improved, silver, and finally it becomes high-value business summaries, gold. It's just like mining. Ore is extracted, then refined, and eventually turned into a valuable medallion. Never forget this saying, what you hold in your hand may be just raw ore, but if refined, it becomes a jewel. Yes, this approach is the philosophy of layer design on the journey of turning data into a jewel. Now let's expand the idea a bit. Friends, the medallion architecture is not an infrastructure architecture, but rather a data design pattern. This means you don't need to install any special software to implement it. The important thing is the discipline of organizing data into layers. The reason we choose a layered structure is to make the data journey more transparent and more manageable. Just as a factory divides production into stages, raw material intake, processing, packaging, medallion divides data into layers. Raw, clean, business ready. So let's go through these layers one by one. Bronze layer, power of raw data. Friends, the bronze layer is the first stop for data. Here, data is stored exactly as it comes from the sources. Log files, IOT device streams, JSON, CSV images, videos, everything is kept directly in this layer. Almost no transformations are applied. Only additional metadata like load date or file name might be added. The advantage of this approach is that you never lose the data history. If in the future someone asks, was this data processed incorrectly? You can always go back to the bronze layer and reuse the original raw data. This increases the system's reliability. You can think of the bronze layer as the warehouse entry point where trucks drop off materials. The materials haven't been washed or sorted yet, but if you want to see the factory's full history, this is the most accurate record. Silver layer, cleaning and organizing. Friends, the silver layer is where the data gains quality. Here, data engineers take the raw data and put it through a series of cleaning steps. Missing values are filled, faulty records are removed, columns are standardized, duplicates are eliminated, and sometimes additional annotations or relationships are added to enrich the data. The most important feature of this layer is that it builds trust in the data. Now analysts and data scientists can confidently use it because it has a defined standard. In a metaphor, the silver layer is like the kitchen counter where vegetables are washed and chopped. Rotten tomatoes are thrown away, the rest are cleaned and sliced. It's not a finished meal yet, but it's ready to be cooked. Gold layer, transforming into business value. Friends, the gold layer is the one most used by the business world. Here, the clean data from the silver layer is summarized, joined, and made ready for business intelligence. For example, daily sales data is aggregated into weekly totals, customer data is segmented, KPI tables are produced. The data in this layer is used directly for reporting, dashboards, and executive decision-making. It is optimized for managers, not for data scientists. The gold layer is like the finished dishes served on elegant plates at the table. At this stage, everything is easy to consume, understandable, and highly valuable. Why do we separate into three layers? There are several key reasons. Traceability, lineage. You can track step-by-step where the data came from, how it was processed, and where it went. Quality management. Each layer ensures quality control. Raw data may be messy, but after silver, it becomes trustworthy. And in gold, it aligns with business logic. Performance. For massive data volumes, reprocessing everything every time is costly. With the medallion structure, only the new, incoming data is processed. Incremental processing. Security. Sensitive data can be stored in the bronze or silver layers, while broader access can be given only to the aggregated data in the gold layer. This way, who sees what data can be controlled more effectively? Who does what? Data engineer. Plays the most critical role in moving data from bronze to silver. They build the ETL slash ELT pipelines and code the data cleaning and transformation processes. Let's briefly explain ETL and ELT, since these two terms often come up when understanding the medallion architecture. They are the approaches used to move and transform data across the layer. ETL. Extract, transform, load. First, data is extracted from source systems. Extract. Then it is cleaned slash transformed. Transform. Finally, it is loaded into the target system. Load. In this case, the lake house. Example. Take sales data coming from a store. Filter out invalid records. Convert all currencies to TL and then load it into the silver layer. ELT. Extract, load, transform. Here, the data is first loaded into the target system. Load. And then transform inside that system. Transform. Example. Load all log files as is into bronze, then use spark code in Databricks to transform them into clean silver data. In summary, ETL. Clean outside or at the source, then load. ELT. Load first, then clean inside the lake house. In modern cloud-based systems like Databricks, ELT is usually preferred because the system is very powerful. It's faster to load the raw data first, then transform it internally, continuing with roles. Ada Stewart, data quality specialist, defines quality rules in the silver layer and ensures standards are applied. Data scientist. Takes the enriched data from the silver layer and develops machine learning or AI model. Data analyst slash BI developer. Uses the aggregated data in the gold layer to create reports and dashboard. Think of the process as a factory production line. Raw material is delivered by logistics. Data engineer. Quality control. Data steward. Inspects and filters it. Product development. Data scientist. Processes it. Sales slash marketing. Analyst slash BI developer. Delivers it to the customer. Final notes. Not every project must have all three layers. Some projects work with just two, for example, bronze plus gold. In some enterprise projects, an additional platinum layer is defined for special, highly critical business reports. What's important is to clearly define each layer's role from the start and apply the discipline consistently. Summary. The medallion architecture is one of the key building blocks of the lake house. It guides data on a structured journey. Bronze stores raw data. Silver improves data quality. Gold transforms it into business value for decision making. Thanks to this layered approach, data becomes traceable, trustworthy, and suitable for different roles. In short, medallion is the journey of turning data from raw ore into a medallion or jewel. All right, friends, I believe the concept is now clear. That concludes today's lesson. See you in the next class. Goodbye for now.

### ACID Transactions & Transaction Logs

Dear friends, hello everyone! Now we are going to look at one of the most important building blocks of the lake house, ACID transactions. In the world of data, reliability is everything. Because companies cannot make decisions based on incorrect, incomplete, or corrupted data. For a data platform to be reliable, it must give us this guarantee. The data here is always consistent, complete, and secure. And this is exactly what the principles we call ACID provide. What is ACID? ACID is an acronym for four fundamental principles. Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability. These were first defined in relational database systems. However, in today's world, especially within the lake house architecture, they have returned very powerfully with Delta Lake. We will examine Delta Lake in detail, but since the topic has come up, I wanted to briefly touch on ACID here. Now let's break down each ACID component one by one. One, Atomicity. Atomicity means that a transaction must either be completed in its entirety or not executed at all. In other words, no half-finished transactions are allowed. Example, imagine transferring money from one bank account to another. If $100 leaves one account but never arrives in the other, the system is faulty. The rule of atomicity says either the money is fully transferred or it never leaves. The same logic applies in data loading scenarios. Suppose you want to load 1,000 rows into a table, but the process fails halfway. Thanks to atomicity, none of those rows are written into the table. This prevents the system from being filled with incomplete or corrupted data. So, Consistency. Consistency means that every transaction must obey the predefined rules of the system. In other words, after a data load is completed, the database must still remain in a valid state. Example, let's say your customer table only accepts positive numbers in the age field. If someone mistakenly enters minus 5 as an age, the consistency rule rejects it. This is especially important in a lake house architecture because data comes from many different sources. Consistency ensures that this data follows the rules, keeping the system valid at all times. Now, the relationship between atomicity and consistency is often confused. For example, a friend might ask, if I enter an invalid value like minus 5 for age, does atomicity or consistency apply here? The answer is, atomicity and consistency work hand in hand. If a single row is invalid, consistency catches it. If the transaction only contains that row, it simply gets rejected. But if there are hundreds of rows in the same transaction, atomicity ensures that either all rows are written or none at all. This prevents the system from becoming inconsistent. Summary, row by row insertion, each row is its own transaction. If there's an error, consistency rejects only that row. While valid rows are written, batch insertion, all rows are one single transaction. If even one row violates the rules, atomicity steps in and says all or nothing. As a result, the entire batch is canceled and no rows are written. All right, I think the concept is clear now. Let's continue with the other components. Three, isolation. Isolation ensures that when multiple transactions happen at the same time, they proceed without interfering with each other. Example, imagine two people trying to buy the same product at the supermarket checkout simultaneously. The cashier processes them one by one until one customer's transaction is complete. The other cannot change the price. The same applies in databases. Two people write to the same table at the same time. The isolation principle ensures they do not see or interfere with each other's operations. This prevents contradictory results in the table. Four, durability. Durability guarantees that once a transaction is successfully completed, the change will be permanent. Even if the system shuts down and restarts, the data will not be lost. Example, you take a photo on your phone and click save. Even if the power goes out, the photo is written into the phone's memory. So when you turn it back on, it's still there. The same is true in the data world. Once a record is added to a table and the transaction is complete, that record is permanent. This ensures that even if the system crashes, the data remains safely stored. In summary, what happens without ACID? Without atomicity. Tables may contain half-written rows, leaving incomplete data. Without consistency, invalid or incorrect data enters the system. Without isolation, concurrent transactions interfere with each other, producing incorrect reports. Without durability, saved data can be lost, causing irreversible damage. These scenarios completely destroy data reliability. In a company, such an environment would put the accuracy of business decisions at serious risk. What is the role of the transaction log? In the lakehouse architecture, ACID principles are enforced through a mechanism called the transaction log. The transaction log records every single action taken. Example, think of it as a flight logbook. Did the plane take off? How many passengers were on board? Who got off? Who got on? Everything is written down step by step. If a problem occurs, you go back and check this logbook. In Delta Lake, the transaction log stores information such as which files were added, which were deleted, and what happened in each version. This enables rolling back faulty data loads, examining previous versions of data, time travel, keeping data consistent even when many people work at the same time. Conclusion, ACID principles are the foundation of reliability in the lakehouse. Thanks to atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability, data is never left incomplete, corrupted, or lost. The transaction log acts as the logbook that enforces these principles. Remember this, no matter how large or diverse the data is, without reliability, it means nothing. ACID makes the lakehouse not only powerful, but also trustworthy. That concludes today's lesson. We'll continue from here in the next session. See you then. Take care.

## Data Governance & Unity Catalog

### From DBFS to Unity Catalog: The Evolution of Data Governance

Dear friends, hello everyone. In this lesson, we will start a new chapter and learn how data is managed in Databricks. Yes, if we think of Databricks as a data platform, its core job is to store data, provide access to it, and manage it securely. But this is not as simple as it sounds. Data can come in many formats, CSV, JSON, images, videos. Some we keep as files while others we want to convert into tables and query with SQL. In other words, there are two different worlds, the file world and the table world. In the early years of Databricks, there were two separate systems to manage these two worlds, DBFS, Databricks File System, and Hive Metastore. Let's now understand these two concepts before moving forward. DBFS, a single window for files. Friends, DBFS is essentially an interface built on top of cloud storages. ADLS in Azure, S3 in AWS, GCS in Google. Normally, accessing these cloud storages can be complicated, but DBFS makes them appear as if they were just a shared folder on your computer. This way, you can directly see, read, and write files. How does cloud storage actually work? Normally, data resides in cloud storages like Azure Data Lake Storage, ADLS, Amazon S3, or Google Cloud Storage, GCS. To access these, you usually need long URLs, access keys, and API calls. In short, reaching a file can be quite complex. So how does DBFS simplify this? DBFS places a middle layer on top of these cloud storages. This layer makes the files appear as if they were on your local disk in a shared folder. For example, normally, to access a file in Azure, you might need a path like this, abfss://container.account.dfs.core. windows.net/.path/.to/.file.csv. With DBFS, you can access the same file like this, dbfs://mnt/.mydata/.file.csv. As you can see, DBFS provides a simpler path. The file still resides in the cloud, but you can access it as if it were on your local disk. Hive Metastore turning files into table. On the other hand, working directly with raw files is not always practical. With a CSV file, unless you define things like this column is X, this data type is integer, this one is date, it's difficult to query it with SQL. That's where Hive Metastore came in. Hive Metastore allowed you to register data as a table. For example, if you define the CSV files in a folder as a sales table, the Metastore records the table name, column names, and data types. Then when you run select asterisk from sales, the system actually reads the files in the background, but you interact with them as if they were a table. You can think of this like a library catalog. There may be hundreds of books on the shelves, but with the catalog, you know where each book is. Hive Metastore worked like a catalog for data. In summary, DBFS managed the files, Hive Metastore managed the tables. It's like one ledger keeping track of inventory while the other tracked accounting. In the beginning, this setup was fine, but over time as company needs grew, it became insufficient. Yes, did you notice? Over time systems automatically evolved. As time went on, it was no longer enough to grant permissions just at the table level. New requirements emerged such as hide this column or only certain users should see this row. It also became necessary to answer the question who accessed which data and when. In other words, auditing became mandatory. Companies wanted to enforce the same governance rules across different cloud environments. Azure, AWS, GCP. There was also a need for lineage, showing where data came from and where it went. But DBFS and Hive Metastore fell short in these areas. They were two separate systems and did not provide a unified solution. That's why Unity Catalog was developed. Unity Catalog brought together the roles of DBFS and Hive Metastore under one umbrella. Now both files and tables are governed by the same system. Along with this, many modern features were introduced. Row and column level access control, for example, masking a customer's personal ID number. Audit logs, who read which table and when. Data lineage, trace data from its source all the way to reports. Multi-cloud and multi-workspace support. One policy, multiple environments. You can think of Unity Catalog as moving all of a company's ledgers into a single centralized accounting system. Now, everyone works in the same system and it's possible to see at a glance where data is and who is using it. Friends, Unity Catalog doesn't just centralize, it also organizes data with a clear hierarchy. You can compare this structure to the governance system of a country or the organizational structure of a university. Let's briefly look at this hierarchy. Metastore, the top layer, the registry of all catalogs, schemas, and tables. Think of it like a national population registry. Catalog sits under the metastore, represents large business units or environments, for example, a finance catalog or a retail catalog. This is like the faculties in a university. Schema lives inside a catalog, smaller subdivisions. For instance, within the finance catalog, you might have an accounts schema or a payroll schema. This is like the departments under each faculty. Tables, views, functions, volume. This is the lowest layer where the actual data objects reside. Table equals structured data like an Excel sheet. View equals filtered or aggregated versions of tables. Function equals small utilities that store reusable calculation logic. Volume equals dedicated storage for files, CSV, JSON images, et cetera. It's very helpful to think of this structure as similar to a university chain. Faculty, department, course, course material. Yes, we will dive deeper into this hierarchy in the upcoming lessons, but let's continue for now. Friends, as you remember, in the medallion architecture, data improved in quality as it moved through the bronze, silver, gold layers. Unity Catalog is the ideal system to organize these layers. Now, here's the problem. These layers are great, but how will a data engineer or analyst know which folder contains which table when they want to access the data? Now, how do we ensure security? That's where Unity Catalog comes in. It places the layers into a clear hierarchy. It lets you control permissions at the layer level. It shows data lineage, which table in bronze transformed into which table in silver and which columns were used in the gold report. Let's say we were working on a retail project. Using the Unity Catalog hierarchy, we define prod.retail underscore bronze, raw data. Example, sales receipts from cash registers, unfiltered. Prod.retail underscore silver, cleaned data. Example, missing customer IDs filled in, date formats standardized. Prod.retail underscore gold, report-ready data. Example, daily sales revenue, top seller products, KPIs. Here, the prod part can represent a catalog at the top level of Unity Catalog. In other words, prod equals the production environment. Underneath, schemas define the bronze slash silver slash gold separation. So what happens? Medallion architecture gives you a data processing flow from raw to business intelligence. Unity Catalog organizes this flow like an organizational chart. Who sees what and where each table came from. This way, it's not just about processing data, but also about delivering it securely in a traceable and organized way. All right, friends, I think the topic is clear. We'll end the lesson here. See you in the next one.

### Understanding Unity Catalog Layers

Dear friends, hello everyone. In the previous lesson, we saw the basic structure of Unity Catalog and touched on it briefly. Do you remember what I said? I told you, we will explore this topic in more detail in a later lesson. Well, here we are now. In this lesson, we'll examine the layers of Unity Catalog. Let's get started. So what did these layers look like in general? At the very top, we had the Metastore, beneath it the Catalog, then the Schema, and at the bottom the Tables, Views, Functions, and Volumes. Yes, in this lesson, we'll take a closer look at each part of this structure. Let's begin. Metastore. The top-level roof. The Metastore acts as Unity Catalog's largest ledger or archive. It stores the record of all catalogs, schemas, and tables. But here's a critical difference. Don't confuse it with the Hive Metastore. In the past, Hive Metastore operated at the workspace level, meaning each workspace had its own separate ledger. Unity Catalog's Metastore, however, operates at the account level. That means you can bring together data from all your workspaces under one roof. We can compare this to a country's Central Population Registry system. In the past, each town kept its own ledger, but now there's a single centralized system. That's why workspaces are no longer isolated from one another. They can all be connected to the same Metastore. Catalog, a new layer. Under the Metastore comes the Catalog, a new concept introduced with Unity Catalog. Hive Metastore did not have this concept. You can think of a catalog as the departments of a large company. For example, one catalog could be finance, another sales, and another HR. Or you could separate them by project environment such as dev, test, and prod. Thanks to catalogs, you can keep data organized by business unit or environment. It's like creating sections within the ledger. Schema the structure under the catalog. Next is the schema, which sits under the catalog. You can map the schema to the database concept in traditional databases. But here's the important note. We are encouraged to use the term schema instead of database. Why? Because the word database can be misleading, making it sound like a completely separate database system. In reality, it's simply a folder-like structure used to group data. Think of it as the relationship in a university. Faculty equals catalog, department equals schema, tables the most common objects. Friends, under the schema, the most commonly used object is the table. Tables are structured data, objects made up of rows and columns. But there are two types of tables, managed and external. Let's briefly touch on them now, and we'll go deeper later. Managed table means Databricks has full control over the data. Both the data itself, files, and the metadata, table definition, column details, et cetera, are stored by Databricks. If you delete the table, not only the definition, but also the underlying files are removed from the cloud. In other words, Databricks owns the data. In an external table, Databricks only stores the metadata, in other words, the identity card of the table. The actual data files remains with the cloud provider. When you delete the table, Databricks removes only the identity card. The actual files stored in the cloud remain untouched. This model is especially useful when consuming data written by other systems. For example, you can define and use as a table in Databricks, the files created by Azure Data Factory or Fivetran. The key difference, managed table equals, Databricks is both the owner and the manager of the data. If you delete it, the files are deleted as well. External table equals, Databricks only keeps the metadata. If you delete it, only the metadata record is removed. The files remain. This distinction is especially important. If you want to produce and manage data directly in Databricks, a managed table makes sense. If you want to use data produced by other systems inside Databricks, an external table is more suitable, as I mentioned. We'll dive into these two table types in more detail in another lesson. For now, this much is enough. Let's move on. Besides tables, Unity Catalog also introduces a new object, volume. Volumes are mainly used to store unstructured files, such as images, JSON files, log records, etc. You can think of this as a storage room. On your desk, you keep documents, tables, but boxes full of files, volumes are stored in the storage room. Thanks to the catalog, you can securely access those files whenever needed. Now, inside a schema, you don't just have tables and volumes. There are also views and functions. View a virtual table derived from existing tables. For example, you can filter only the last 30 days from a sales table and create a view. Function allows you to package and store frequently repeated calculations. For instance, instead of writing the same date conversion logic every time, you define a function. These are helpful tools that make your work life much easier. All right, we've understood these topics. Now let me share an anecdote. There's one more important point. With the arrival of Unity Catalog, Hive Metastore didn't completely disappear. Databricks provides backward compatibility. In every workspace, there is still a built-in pseudo-catalog called hive underscore metastore. You can continue creating tables there out of habit. However, for new projects, the recommended approach is to use Unity Catalog. Because Hive Metastore lacks modern features such as column-level access control, audit logs, and lineage. Friends, I will demonstrate this in practice, but let me explain it theoretically as well. With Unity Catalog, when accessing a table, you now need to use three-level naming in the format. Catalog dot schema dot table. For example, finance dot sales dot customers. Here, finance, catalog, sales, schema, customers, table. In Hive Metastore, sometimes two levels, schema dot table, were enough. But with Unity Catalog, we get a clearer, more structured, and more secure approach. To summarize, in this lesson, we explored Unity Catalog's hierarchy in more detail. Metastore works as an account-level umbrella. Catalog is a new concept introduced with Unity Catalog. Schema is preferred, instead of the old-term database. Tables can be either managed or external. Volumes are used for storing files. Views and functions are helpful supporting tools. Hive Metastore still exists, but with limited functionality. We now access data using a three-level naming structure. This way, we've clarified the details behind the bigger picture we saw in the previous lesson. We'll continue from here in the next lesson. See you soon. Take care.

### Managed vs External Tables in Unity Catalog

Dear friends, hello everyone. As you know, in the previous lesson, while exploring the Unity Catalog layers, we came across a certain layer. We also noted that this layer has two parts, managed and external tables. Yep, we didn't go into much depth, but only touched on these topics at a surface level. Now we are going to examine these two in detail, because once we move from theory to practice, I don't want you to feel unfamiliar with how things work in the application. So, without wasting time, let's get started. Friends, when you create a table in Databricks, you are not just creating a queryable object, the same time you are making a decision about the ownership and life cycle of the data. This decision affects everyday questions such as, when I drop the table, should the files be deleted as well? Can I share the same data with another ETL tool? Who manages the cost? In short, whether you choose managed or external tables will shape the way you work, just like the difference between renting an office and owning one outright. A managed table means that Databricks manages both the identity of the data, metadata, and the data itself, files. When we think of a table, we are actually talking about two separate things. The data itself, which are the files that contain the records, row by row for example, values like joseph-25-stockhole, and the identity of the data, meaning the metadata that describes it, the table name, which columns it has, the data types of those columns, and in which schema and catalog it resides. You can think of metadata like an ID card. The card doesn't contain the person themselves, but it holds descriptive information such as their name, date of birth, and ID number. In Databricks, if you are using a managed table, both the metadata and the actual data are managed by Databricks. When you drop the table, both the identity and the content disappear together. An external table, on the other hand, is a model where Databricks only keeps the ID card, metadata. The files themselves remain in an external location and are often shared with other systems as well. Here, Databricks acts like a tenant when you turn off the lights and leave drop. The house itself remains, the table definition is deleted, but the files stay untouched. That's why external tables are ideal when you want to simply register and use data in Databricks that was written by external systems like ADF or Fivetran. So where do we make this choice? Friends, the decision about what kind of table it will be is made at the moment you create the table. Under unity catalog, if you create a table with create table without specifying a location, it becomes managed because Databricks writes the data into its own default managed location. If you provide an explicit folder path with location, dot, dot, dot, then the table becomes external. The metadata is stored in UC while the files remain in the cloud path you pointed to. So the practical intuition is no location equals managed. Specify a location equals external and unity catalog managed tables are always Delta format. You cannot create managed tables in parquet slash CSV slash Jason. For those formats, you must use an external table. Yes, in managed tables, the life cycle is fully controlled by Databricks end to end schema evolution. Maintenance operations like optimize slash Z order, vacuum and retention policies are all centrally managed. When you drop the table, the files are also deleted. In other words, the cleaning crew is included in the same contract. For external tables, Databricks acts only as a registry clerk, it updates the table definition and runs performance optimizations. But you are responsible for the physical lifecycle of the files. Even if you drop the table, you still need to delete the file separately on the cloud. This difference is similar to asking, are all the construction and maintenance jobs handled by a single contractor, or are they shared with the building owner? Both table types benefit from unity catalogs are back column masking audit and lineage features. We'll explore these both theoretically and practically. In short, questions like who can access what and how are solved centrally by UC. The key distinction grows on the storage authorization side. An external table in UC is authorized via external location plus storage credential. And Databricks only has access to that folder within the scope of the permissions granted. This is highly valuable in environments that require organizational separation. For example, when producer systems write the files, and Databricks is only allowed to read them. In a managed table, UC handles storage permissions automatically on your behalf. You proceed with a single door single lock model. Yes, the managed model provides operational comfort for data platform teams who want Databricks to handle everything in the ecosystem. So they can just focus on their work, storage path, folder organization, cleanup policies, checkpoint slash log retention, all are centrally managed. And billing visibility is clear to data is in one place. The external model, on the other hand, may store data under different teams or accounts. This makes it ideal for scenarios like internal cost separation or shared data lake. However, the responsibility for file cleanup and lifecycle remains with you. Meaning you consciously choose to keep part of that responsibility outside Databricks. Good news, Delta Lake features, ACID, transaction log, time travel, merge slash delete slash update, optimize, Z order, CDF are independent of the table type. What matters is that the table is Delta. Whether the table is managed or external does not directly determine query speed. The real difference comes from clustering slash computation, regular maintenance, optimize slash vacuum, and the data model. In practice, however, managed tables integrate more quickly into maintenance and standardization workflows. Well, for external tables, the file lifecycle depends on your discipline. It's like keeping the same engine in two different garages. The engine gives the same power, but the garage's organization affects how easy maintenance is. In real life teams, this approach is comfortable. In the bronze layer, especially raw data written by external systems, tables are often external because it fits the source systems I write you consume logic. In the silver layer, cleaned and standardized data is mostly managed because keeping it in Databricks managed space makes optimization and maintenance easier and ELT workflows faster. In the gold layer, analytical slash BI tables are also typically managed. So report reproducibility and cleanup policies are centrally handled. This creates a clear boundary, raw data external process data internal. So what did we say? When you first create a table, you decide whether it will be managed or external. For example, whether you provide a location in the create table command. That decision applies only to that specific table. In your data pipeline, you will need other tables too, and you will make the choice again for each. In medallion architecture, bronze, silver, and gold are actually separate tables. Bronze, raw data ingested from the source into a table, often external because the files already come from an external source. For example, IOT system or ETL tool. Silver data from bronze is cleaned and written into a new table. Making it managed makes sense because keeping it in a Databricks managed space makes optimization and cleanup easy. Gold aggregates and report tables are created from silver. These are generally managed for long-term maintenance, performance, and easier data sharing. Let's continue. External tables facilitate data sharing across platforms. For example, when the same files are read by Databricks and an MPP warehouse, because you connect to a shared cloud folder via a contracted access model IM slash ACL. Managed tables, on the other hand, simplify sharing within Databricks via delta sharing or secure views. It's like one-click sharing for internal teams. In short, external enhances cross-platform sharing while managed enhances internal simple sharing. Two critical warnings to remember. If you drop a managed table, the files are deleted as well. This is a conscious irreversible choice. Do not directly delete or manipulate files in the folder behind an external table. In a delta table, all changes must go through delta commands. Otherwise, the transaction log and data files will become inconsistent and the table will lose integrity. This is like taking money from a cash register without updating the ledger. The records won't match. Friends, sometimes you may want to convert an external delta table into a managed table, for example, to simplify maintenance. The usual way to do this, if it's delta, is to copy it into a managed location using methods like deep clone or CTAS, create table as select. The reverse, managed external, involves writing the data to an external target and creating a new external table. The main idea, instead of changing the table type like a label, it's cleaner to recreate the data according to the rules of the target type. Practical compass when deciding. If you produce data inside Databricks and want to manage it centrally, silver slash gold layers, frequent maintenance, frequent merge slash optimize, centralized governance, clear lifecycle, stick with managed tables. It's like having a single contractor managing a well-organized site. If data will be produced or consumed by other systems, storage is managed by a separate account slash team, and you want the file lifecycle to stay there, choose an external table. Think of it like a shared space on a shared campus. Both approaches are valid. You are deciding where ownership should reside. In short, managed VS external is not just a technical detail. It's an operational strategy. Managed tables provide a world where Databricks is the homeowner. External tables provide a world where Databricks is the tenant. In a medallion journey, most organizations operate with minimal friction by keeping raw data external and processed slash value added layers managed. This way, you leverage Delta's ACID guarantees while managing your data consistently, securely, and traceably through Unity Catalog's governance framework. Yes, this topic may seem a bit complex, but for now, understanding the logic is enough. We will do practical exercises later, and it will become completely clear. That's all for this lesson. See you in the next one. Take care.

### Creating a Unity Catalog

All right, my friends. Hello, everybody. Welcome. Welcome. It is time to get down to practice. So what are we going to do exactly? We will create a Unity catalog on Databricks free edition. So why don't we just get started? So you can see I'm already on Databricks. From the menu on the left, I can go to the catalog option. Let's click on that and see what we got. So you can see some catalogs already appear by default, right? System or workspace. These are just starting points that are automatically provided by Databricks with this free edition. Thank you very much. So understanding what they are is very important. So it doesn't get too confusing in the next couple of steps. All right. So let's just start with this system catalog. Right. So this system catalog is kind of like a notebook where Databricks keeps its own system records. So it does not contain your tables or data. Just need to be clear. But instead, it's got all the information about the system itself. Right. Which tables have been created, which users have access or audit and lineage details. And this is about how the data has been processed. So in your daily work, you really won't be using this much, especially in the free edition. But in the large enterprise projects, this kind of information is going to be critical. So, for example, when your manager asks you who access this report, not that you have manager like that, but you know. Anyway, the answer does come right from the records in the system catalog. Cool. Now, let's move on to the workspace catalog. So the workspace catalog is where your own tables and schemas are saved by default in this free edition. ### Creating Volumes – Lesson 1

All right, all right, hello my friends, welcome back. So far, we've been uploading and exploring our data through tables. Tables allows us to run SQL queries, perform cleaning, make transformations on the data. However, in the real world, data does not only come in table form. Most of the time, it comes from external systems as raw files like CSV, JSON, log files, even images or PDFs. This is where volumes come into play. So you can think of volumes as a file storage system provided by Databricks. We can directly upload files here and read them using Spark or SQL. In this way, as students, we're going to be able to learn not only how to work with tables, but also with raw files. That means for now, we will also upload the same datasets related to orders and products into volumes. In this way, we're going to have two different sources. Now, you may have noticed we uploaded this same data both under tables and under volumes. Now, first glance, might seem unnecessary, but this was intentional because I want you to just have a better understanding of the logic of file uploading and management in Databricks. See, so when we upload on the table side, the data is automatically converted into Delta format. We can query it directly with SQL. This is a very powerful method for daily analysis and reporting as it turns out. But on the volume side, the data remains in its raw file format. So in other words, we store CSV or JSON files as they are. From there, we can read them with Spark using their file paths. So this method actually reflects a scenario that data engineers frequently encounter in the real world. Often data first comes as files, then it's processed and converted into tables. So therefore, by uploading the same data in two places, I'm actually helping you see two different approaches side-by-side. Cool. Now, here's a table approach. For table, it's ready for direct analysis. The file approach and volumes provides practice in working with raw data. So in the following lessons upcoming, we're going to read the files and volumes with Spark, perform small transformations, and thus experience the journey from file through analysis. ## Getting Started with ETL Apache Spark

### Getting Started with ETL and Apache Spark

Well, hello there, my friends. Welcome back. So, right now, we need to begin an entirely new section. One of the fundamental tasks in data engineering is to gather data from different sources, right? Then process it and prepare it for analysis. This process is actually called ETL, extract, transform, load. So, in short, it consists of extracting the data from its source, transforming it according to requirements, and then loading it into the target system. Now, in modern data platforms, ETL is the primary mechanism for improving data quality, as well as enabling business units to access reliable reporting, okay? Now, the Databricks environment provides a natural platform for ETL processes because Databricks combines the power of the Spark engine with a cloud-based lakehouse architecture. The Apache Spark is a very powerful framework and is capable of processing massive datasets in parallel. So, using the Spark DataFrame API, or Spark SQL, you can perform ETL operations on both structured data, CSV, JSON, Parquet, and semi-structured data, nested JSON, arrays, maps. You follow? Yeah, so Databricks makes these processes even easier with features like Autoloader, Delta Live Tables, and Unity Catalog. Both ingestion and transformation steps are accelerated. Now, to truly understand ETL, it's really important to remember the concept of the medallion architecture. You remember that? Data within a lakehouse is typically divided into three layers. That would be bronze, silver, and gold. All right, so don't worry, I'm going to be repeating this so many times, you'll never forget it. In fact, you're going to want me to shut up, which you probably already do. So, let's keep moving. The bronze layer stores raw data, often in the same form it comes from the source system, for example, CSV or JSON files. In the silver layer, this data is cleaned, transformed, and joined. So, null values are handled, type conversions are performed, duplicate records are removed, and additional columns required for business processes are created. That's all in the silver layer. The gold layer contains summarized or enriched data sets designed for business intelligence as well as reporting needs. See, so each transition between these layers essentially represents an ETL process. Now, one of the most critical steps in ETL is data validation and cleaning. So, raw data often contains errors, missing values, or conflicting records. You know this already, I'm sure. For example, customer data may show the same email address linked to multiple customer records, or order tables might have null delivery dates. So, it's during ETL, identifying these issues, removing duplicate records, and filling in missing values, or even deleting them if necessary. This is the engineer's responsibility. So, we're basically ensuring that the data written to the silver layer becomes much more reliable. Now, another important stage, though, is transformation. See, business processes often require data in a format different than the raw input, as you might have guessed or have experienced. So, for example, in an order items table, well, you may need to create a new column to calculate each product's total cost, such as price plus freight value, or you may need to convert date columns from string format into timestamp type. Now, see, Spark supports these kinds of transformations through its functional API. Using functions like with column, filter, group by, and ag, you can perform simple and complex transformations. And for more advanced needs, you can define UDFs, or user-defined functions, in order to apply custom business rules. And then for the final stage of ETL, load, this is the process of writing data into the target layer. So, in the Databricks world, this is usually done using the Delta format. So, the Delta Lake format only provides the compression and columnar advantages of Parquet, but also delivers powerful features such as ACID transitions, schema enforcement, and time travel. So, it's thanks to these capabilities, the loading process is well protected against issues like did duplicates occur, or is my date column in the wrong data type, right? So, there's more. Merge operations in Delta Lake make it way easier to handle upsert, which is update and insert scenarios. And then from a certification perspective, ETL processes are also highly important. See, the Databricks Certified Data Engineer Associate exam tests a candidate's fundamental knowledge and skills in ETL. So, the participants are expected to know how to read CSV, JSON, and even binary files with Spark, also how to connect to relational databases via JDBC, and how to apply basic transformations with the DataFrame API. Additionally, removing duplicate records, handling null values, creating UDFs, and writing transformed data into Delta tables are all topics directly covered in the exam. So, ETL process is one of the most essential skills both in the real business world and in certification exams. So, that's why the goal of this lesson is to not only introduce students to the ETL concept theoretically, but also demonstrate how it is implemented on Spark and Databricks. So, in the next step, we will use the OLIST dataset to apply a real ETL pipeline through this bronze-silver-gold flow, and we'll do it step by step. This way, we'll internalize the ETL concept both as preparation for the exam and as a practical business skill. All right, my friends, that's about as clear as I can make it. So, we'll wrap it up here, but I want to see you next time. All right, goodbye for now.

### External Tables: Using External Data Without Bringing It into Databricks

All right, hello my friends and welcome back. So up until this point, we've learned the concept of a managed table, right? Yeah. So when we create a managed table, the data is coming under Databricks' control. Okay, so if we drop the table, the data is also deleted. Now, we also said that this model is very useful when we want Databricks to have full control of the data. However, in real life, not every data set is uploaded directly into Databricks. See, most of the time data is generated by other systems, an ETL tool, such as Fivetran, Azure Data Factory, application log files, or CSV, or JSON files shared by other teams. So copying this data again into Databricks can be both costly and unnecessary. See, this is exactly where external tables come in. So in our OLIS dataset, we will not be using external tables though. That's why I'm not gonna be demonstrating this part for you. I just wanna let you know what's going on. Since there is a chance that it may appear in the certification exam, I just wanted to include it in this particular curriculum theoretically, all right? So let's do a rundown and see what we got. So what were we talking about? An external table, right? Gives a table view to files stored in an external location. So that's outside of Databricks. So yeah, the data stays where it is. Well, Databricks only creates a metadata record. Okay, I just wanna be clear about that. So this metadata defines the table name, column names, data types, the file format being used and the file location. So when we query the table using SQL, Databricks reads the files and presents them to us just as if they were a table, okay? So now, how is an external table actually defined then? I'm here to tell you. So the basic SQL statement used to create an external table goes like this. You can see the example code on the screen, but I do wanna go through this SQL code step-by-step with you. So create table. Yeah, creates a new table. If not exists, prevents recreating the table if it does already exist. Okay, so here we are creating the table. Of course, we will need to define the table within the unity catalog hierarchy, right? Catalog, schema, table name. So here you can see I've added this sample structure, catalog.schema.logs. Next, we write the column names and the data types since the file does not have a header. Now, my friends, because we define the metadata ourselves in an external table, we can actually specify the column names and data types in here. So let's say, for example, we have a column called log underscore ID and its type is integer. You can also see the other columns defined here. And we're moving on with using CSV. Yeah, we specify the file format. With options, we define additional settings. And also, my friends, when we're creating an external table, the options clause actually allows it to specify how Databricks should read the file. Because each file format like CSV, JSON, Parquet, et cetera, they all have different properties, right? That makes sense. So for example, one of the most common options for CSV files is header. So the header parameter tells Spark whether the first row of the file contains column names or not. So if we set header equals true, well, Spark treats the first row as column names and the columns of our table are derived from these names. If we were to set header equals false, Spark automatically will assign names like underscore C0, C1, C2. You remember that from before. And that means that we need to define the schema manually. All right, so similarly, the delimiter parameter specifies which character separates values within a row. The default delimiter is a comma, but in some files it might be a semicolon comma, a pipe, or even a backslash T for tab. So if we don't actually specify the correct delimiter, the entire row could be read as a single column. That wouldn't be good. So in short, we define whichever delimiter is actually used in the file so that Spark can read it correctly. So beyond this, the options clause allows many more configurations. So let's have a look at some of the most common ones. Encoding specifies a character set of the file, for example, UTF-8, ISO 8859-1. Now, this is important for working properly with different alphabets. Pay attention. Null value. This defines the special expression that represents missing values in the file, for example, null or NA. Spark will automatically treat these, by the way, as null. Quote and escape. This controls how quotation marks or special characters inside the data are handled. Multiline. Some JSON or CSV files may store a single record across multiple lines. So setting multiline equals true would tell Spark to combine those lines into one record. So basically, options let us provide Spark with the settings that match the structure of the file. Especially for CSV files, the header and the limiter are gonna be the most common and critical ones. So if we don't define them correctly, we cannot properly load the data into a table. Now, we're coming up to the most critical part here, and this is very important. Ah, what is it? Location. So my friends, this points to the external folder where the files are stored. So this line is what makes a table external, right? And as you can see from here, there's a directory path to an external folder, okay? So in other words, once we write and execute this code, our table's gonna be ready. But how can we check, see whether the table is external or managed? We can use this command, describe extended catalog.schema.logs. So this command returns all the metadata of the table. So if the output shows type external, then our table is indeed external. We can also see which location that it's linked to. But let me ask you, what would happen if the files change? Well, files outside may be deleted, or new ones may be added, of course. External tables do not always detect these changes automatically, and that's why we do need to refresh the metadata. And for this, we can use the refresh table statement with the table's path, okay? So refresh table catalog.schema.logs. So my friends, this command re-scans the list of files under the table. If new files have been added, they get included. If files have been deleted, they get removed from the metadata. And then, yeah, what if we were wanting to drop a table? On that case, we can use the drop table statement with the path, drop table catalog.schema.logs. So when we do this, only the metadata in Unity Catalog is deleted. The external files in storage remain untouched. And that, my friends, is the main advantage of an external table. Copy that.
