### Detecting Duplicate Keys in the Bronze Layer

All right, all right, hello, my dear friends, and welcome back. In the previous lesson, if you remember, we were looking at the general information of the data sets, and we made some notes from our analysis. And remember, we noted that detecting duplicate records is important, especially ensuring the primary key column in each data set does not contain duplicates. So now we need to check on whether this condition is satisfied. So in this video, we're going to focus on one of the most fundamental quality checks in the entire bronze layer, detecting duplicate keys. Now as you may know, every table has a primary key column. For example, in the orders table, it's order ID. In the customers table, it's customer ID. And in the products table, yeah, product ID. So these columns should be unique for every row, right? So if an order customer product ID is repeated, then the analyses we perform later on in the silver and gold layers may produce incorrect results. And since the purpose of the bronze layer is not to change the data, but to take notes, here we only ask the following questions. Well, how many total rows are there in this table? How many unique values are there based on the key columns? The difference between the total and the unique count shows us how many duplicates exist. Then this way, if duplicates are found, we record this situation. For example, if the orders table contains the same order ID multiple times, this means we have a problem that we must clean later in the silver stage. Now in some tables, we also use composite keys, and that just means uniqueness is ensured by a combination of two columns instead of just one. So say for example, in the order items table, order ID plus order item ID. In the order payments table, order ID plus payment sequential. So you see this way, individual items with an order or individual payments for an order can then be distinguished. So again, we apply the same logic, compare the total number of rows with a number of unique combinations. Okay, so basically in this lesson, we'll check whether there were duplicates in the key columns during the bronze stage. Now if duplicates exist, we take note, but we do not delete them yet. In the silver stage, we will clean these duplicates to make the data more reliable. Okay, let's get started. So what I'm doing now is, I'll create a new dictionary structure and assign it to a variable named data frames. Yeah, so I'm pasting the dictionary here to save some time. So in this structure, the keys are the names that we'll later use as identifiers. The values are tuples containing two elements. The first is the data frame itself, and the second is the list of key columns we want to check for duplicates. So soon, we will use these elements inside of a loop to run our checks. So now I'm going to add a simple comment. You remember it? Hash, simple duplicate check, and I'll start a loop with, for name, in parentheses, df, keys, in data frames dot items, open and close parentheses, colon. All right, so this way, we'll iterate through each data set and its key columns to perform the duplicate check. Now, my friends, through the items method, the tuple structure will be passed directly into the variables in order. Name will hold the dictionary keys, while the tuple on the right will provide the pairs. All right? So now let's move on to the body of the loop. First, I'll create a variable called total and call the count function on the data frame. Now, my friends, in Spark, count is an action, so it scans all partitions across a cluster and then returns the total row count. Yeah, so now we have the total number. Next, I'll create another variable called distinct. Now, on the data frame, I'll apply the select function and pass in star keys. Now, the star or unpack operator in Python expands a list, like order ID or whatever, into individual arguments for the function. See, this way, each key column will be selected one by one. And right after that, I'll apply the distinct function. So what do you think this is going to do? It actually deduplicates the selected key columns. So for example, if there are, let's say, 10 identical values, it's going to treat them as a single unique value. Follow? Yeah. So finally, let's count them. So I call count again, and this gives us a number of unique key combinations. So the total shows the total number of rows. Distinct shows the deduplicated count. And here's the logic. If all the keys are unique, then the distinct count will equal the total row count. And of course, if there's a difference, it means duplicates exist. Now I'll just add a little formatting to display the results. Inside a print statement, I'll use an f-string and convert the name value to uppercase with dot upper. And I'll show the values. Total equals total in curly braces. Distinct keys equals distinct in curly braces. Duplicates equals in curly braces, total minus distinct. And this way, the output will directly display our results. Now it is important to remember here, distinct treats null values as valid. If the key columns contain null, multiple rows with null are considered a single unique value. So if your data set has nulls in key columns, the duplicate count may appear lower than it actually is. Now in the bronze stage, we usually just take note of this. And then later in silver, we handle it with rules like exclude rows where the key is null or fix missing keys. There's a few others. All right. So let's run the code. ### Payments Data Validation and Transformation – Lesson 2

Well, hello my friends, welcome back. So in this lesson, before we go moving on to the silver layer, we'll discuss the final step we need to take to ensure data integrity, duplicate checking, meaning the detection of repeated records. So in data engineering, one of the most fundamental ways to measure a data set's quality is to check whether the same record appears more than once. Because duplicate rows can lead to incorrect totals, inaccurate averages, and misleading reports. Therefore, performing a duplicate check when moving from bronze to silver acts almost like a data quality insurance. So what does a duplicate mean in the payments table? Well, you see this order payments table contains payment details for each order. And sometimes an order is represented by a single payment row, sometimes multiple payment rows. For example, a customer may pay part of their order with a credit card and let's say the remaining part with a coupon. So seeing the same order ID appear multiple times is going to be completely normal. However, here's the key distinction. If the same payment sequence, that's payment sequential, appears more than once within the same order, that's incorrect. Because a single order should have only one first payment, one second payment, and so on. So if the same sequence number occurs multiple times for the same order, that likely indicates a duplicate record caused during data loading. Therefore, we'll perform the duplicate analysis by checking the relationship between two variables, order underscore ID and payment underscore sequential. Let's go ahead and write the code. This is what we'll start with. Select order underscore ID comma payment underscore sequential to select the columns. Then we'll use count star to count how many records exist for each combination of these columns. So I'll name this count as CNT using as CNT. Now let's choose our table. I type from followed by the data set. Next I add group by and include both columns there. Now my friends, this groups the rows by the order plus payment sequence pair. Yeah, each unique combination of order ID payment sequential becomes one group. Then we can use count star to see how many rows exist within each group. Now some of you might be scratching your head and asking, well, why wouldn't checking only order ID be enough? Well the answer is no, because order ID represents an order, yeah, but a single order can have multiple payments. For example, take a look at the table below. See here the same order ID appears twice, but that's perfectly fine since a customer made two separate payments. Therefore checking for duplicates based only on order ID would definitely mislead us, right? It would give us a false data error warning. But in the same way, checking only the payment sequential would also be incorrect, and that's because different orders can share the same sequence number. So let's say, for example, both orders A001 and A002 may have payment sequential equaling one, and that's completely valid. So the real uniqueness is going to be defined by the combination of order ID and payment sequential. So in other words, each payment sequence within an order must be unique. Yes, if the same sequence number appears twice for a single order, then one of those rows is an unnecessary duplicate. So with this query, the system is essentially asking, within each order, order ID, has the same payment sequence, payment sequential, appeared more than once? If the query returns any results, those rows are considered duplicates in the dataset. And in that case, before moving on to the silver layer, we would either filter or flag the data so that each order keeps only one payment sequence. So this check is just as important as cleaning the data directly. Because sometimes, instead of deleting duplicate records, we prefer to mark them, for example, is duplicate equals true, and simply exclude them from analyses later. Transparency. All right, my friends, let's continue. It's all right, having count star in parentheses greater than one, right? So this applies a filter on the grouped results, and it means return only the groups where the number of rows is greater than one. So it's selecting the groups where the same payment sequence appears more than once within the same order. In other words, the duplicates. I do want you to make note of having works after group by, which is why we use having instead of where. Because where cannot filter aggregate functions like count star. And finally, I can write order by, CNT, DESC, and this will sort the results in descending order. You see, this way, the most frequently repeated combinations, the most problematic ones, will appear at the top. All right, let's go ahead and run the code. All right, well, no results were returned, and that means there's no issue. So we won't need to perform any additional work at the silver layer. But do you see how important it is, right? We now saw that duplicate checking isn't just a technical step, it's actually a fundamental part of ensuring data reliability. But we also learned why neither order ID nor payment sequential alone would be sufficient, and how checking both together provides the most logical and business-accurate approach. And though we didn't encounter any duplicates, we now fully understand the logic and the workflow behind the code. So from now on, we can be confident that every table used in the silver layer consists only of verified and unique rows. Well, hello my friends, welcome back! Thanks for hanging in there, you're doing really good work. Now, as you know, in the previous video we completed the processing of three columns. What are we going to do? Well, the step we'll perform next is called the Centroid Geographical Center step. And it's with this operation we'll generate a single representative latitude-longitude value for each postcode, that's the zip prefix. So the goal here is to take the multiple and slightly different coordinate points in the bronze layer and represent them with a single coordinate in the silver layer. See, this way we'll have a clean, join-ready lookup table that follows the rule, one zip underscore prefix equals one row. But what's our purpose? Well, in the geolocation table, the same zip prefix appears multiple times with slightly different latitude-longitude values. These duplicates create noise in analytics and join operations. In the silver layer, we want just one point per postal code. And the most practical and consistent way to achieve this is to take the average of all points that belong to each postal code. That's going to be our centroid. Okay? So this approach helps us to obtain a central point without large deviation from the actual geographic distribution. It also merges duplicate rows into a single record and eliminates ambiguity in joins we'll perform with customer or seller tables based on postal codes. Okay? So you're ready to start? Let's do it. First, let's create a temporary table by writing create or replace temp view centroids, and then I'll continue with as select and select the columns. Because having multiple lat and longitude values for the same zip prefix simply means that this postal code covers several nearby measurement points. That's all. So all of these coordinates are within the same regional boundary. They're very close to each other. So when we take their average, we obtain the point closest to the geographical center of that area. In other words, the average becomes the most logical representative point for that postal code. Now, in some places you might also see a function simply called rank. That one also gives the same rank to equal values, but it skips the next number. So, for example, for that ten, eight, eight, seven, it would assign one, two, two, four. So in our case, we'll use dense rank. And here I'll use over now, what's over going to do here? In SQL, the over clause allows you to apply an aggregation function like some average or rank. Without grouping the data, but instead over a defined window of rows. So inside over, I'll define the ordering. I write order by seller underscore count and then add descending. DESC, of course, means it will sort from highest to lowest. So instead of having to rewrite the same query every time, defining it as a function helps us avoid code duplication, and it standardizes our analyses. Now, there are three main types of functions in Databricks Unity Catalog. We've got the scalar function. These functions return a single value, such as a number, ratio, or percentage. For example, scalar functions are used to calculate the average sales percentage of revenue from a specific category, or even delivery delay rate. Table function. Yeah, these functions return an entire table, meaning results are produced in rows and columns. And they're typically used to generate filtered subsets or summary reports based on certain conditions. For instance, a function that lists orders paid with credit card or sales within a specific date range would be a table function example. But this third type is called user-defined function, UDF. So these are functions that are completely defined by the user and perform custom operations. So UDFs are used for special calculations, text processing, or data transformations based on specific business rules. These would be cases that cannot be solved using built-in functions. For example, a function that automatically calculates a sentiment score from customer reviews. That would be a good example of a UDF. ### Designing Analytical Joins in the Gold Layer

Well, hello, my friends, and welcome back. So in this lesson, after completing the analyses we've performed on the orders table within the gold layer, we'll now learn how to combine our data from different perspectives to gain deeper insights. Now since you already understand the logic and the purpose of this topic, I don't want to go through a full coding exercise. Instead, I just want to share a few examples to give you some inspiration. This way, you'll not only have a clear conceptual understanding of the topic, but also a roadmap to guide your future analyses. Yeah, let's get to it. So of course, at this stage, our goal is no longer just to study order behavior. We want to understand the customers, sellers, products, geographies, and time dimensions behind those orders. So this is the point where, in the gold layer, we move into analytical modeling, where data starts to tell the business story. So first, customer-centric join. We'll start with a customer-centric join structure. And this approach merges data around customers by combining the customers' orders, order payments, and order reviews tables. With this join, we can analyze each customer's purchasing behavior. For example, how often does a customer shop? How much do they spend on average? How satisfied are they with the products they buy? So using this analysis, we can calculate the average order value per customer, identify repeat customers, and even define high-value customers' groups. So in the gold layer, this join can be transformed into a table, such as customer performance or customer lifetime value, which helps measure customer loyalty and long-term engagement. Next, we'll focus on the seller-centric join. So this join combines a seller's order items, orders, and order reviews tables. So the goal here would be to analyze seller performance, examining each seller's total sales, average delivery time, and customer satisfaction. So as a result, we can see which sellers deliver faster and which ones receive higher customer ratings. So this structure would be especially valuable for assessing logistics quality and supply chain efficiency. See, in the gold layer, this join can be turned into a table called seller performance, helping the business evaluate the overall quality of its marketplace. The third structure is the product or category analytics join. So here we would combine the product, order items, category lookup, and order reviews tables. The goal here would be to examine the relationships between sales, popularity, and satisfaction at the product and category level. And through this analysis, we could identify which categories sell the most, which products receive the highest ratings, and which ones are returned most frequently. And the results obtained from this join can be used to shape marketing strategies, optimize inventory management, for instance. And in the gold layer, this analysis can be transformed into a table called category performance. Then comes our fourth type of join, which would be geolocation-based joins. And this join involves the geolocation, customers, orders, and sellers tables. So the main goal here would be to understand the impact of geography on delivery performance. So delivery times could be compared by city or state to answer questions like, in which regions is order density higher, in which regions are deliveries faster? We can also uncover the relationship between customer-seller distance and delivery time. So this structure can be transformed into a table named regional performance, or even logistics efficiency in the gold layer, and then can be used for route planning or delivery optimization. In the fifth stage, we'll focus on payment behavior joins. So this join combines the order payments, orders, and customers tables. And the goal, of course, would be to analyze customer payment behavior. So it helps us answer questions like, which payment methods are used most frequently, under which payment types is the average order value higher, what is the relationship between installment count and total spending? Then, of course, the analysis can be transformed into a table named payment behavior, which can then be used both in financial decision support systems and marketing segmentation. Friends, for many years, the dominant approach in data engineering has been batch processing, which I just mentioned in the previous question. In this approach, we first collect the data and then process it in bulk at specific intervals. At the end of the day, we generate reports, do weekly analyses, and create monthly summary tables. In a way, this approach was like loading products onto a truck and taking them to a warehouse at the end of the day. So, what do we do until the truck is full? We wait, then we proceed. Batch processing is easy to understand, friends. It's also relatively simple to implement, and for a long time, it met the needs of the business world. However, as we entered the modern world and the speed of data production increased, this approach started to fall short because today, the value of data lies not only in its accuracy, but also in its timeliness. So, why is batch processing no longer sufficient? Friends, in many business scenarios today, tomorrow is already too late. In modern systems, data is produced continuously, flows nonstop, and loses its value very quickly, friends. IoT sensors, online transactions, log records, mobile applications, financial activities, all of these actually generate a continuous stream of data. At this point, batch processing is like collecting water from a constantly running tap with a bucket once a day. The water keeps flowing, but you only notice it at certain intervals. This is where the idea of streaming comes into play. In other words, it's the idea of never-ending data. So, what is a stream? Dear friends, a data stream is a flow of data with no boundaries. With batch data, you say, this data set is complete, now I can process it. But in streaming, there is no such moment. The data keeps flowing, it keeps coming in. Today, data comes in, and tomorrow, even more will come. An hour later, even more could come in. The stream never really ends. We can think of this as a metaphor, like a river. Batch processing is like taking a snapshot of the river, while streaming is like watching the river flow. A photo is clear, but it's static. A stream is alive, but it's harder to manage. Yeah, now the concept has taken shape in our minds. Now that we understand this topic, we can dive a little deeper. Friends, Spark Structured Streaming is a fundamental concept. Instead of treating streaming as a complicated special case, Spark Structured Streaming handles it with a model that's very similar, almost identical to batch processing. This is where Spark's revolutionary idea comes in, and it's this. Think of a stream, that is, flowing data, as a continuously growing table. In other words, streaming data. It's like a table where new rows are constantly being added. Yesterday, 100 rows were added to the table. Today, 1,000 more rows could be added. Tomorrow, that number will keep increasing, again and then. The table grows, but you work with it, using the same data frame logic. This approach makes streaming much more manageable mentally, because what do data engineers already do? They work with tables. They work with the data frame logic, and that's how we've been working so far, too. We're used to thinking this way. Now, let's talk about why batch and streaming feel so similar. Yeah, our main question is this. Why do batch and streaming feel so similar? Guys, the biggest advantage of structured streaming is this. In streaming, you use almost the same data frame APIs that you use in batch. For example, operations like select, filter, with column, and group by work the same way for both batch and streaming. This means the following. Except for a small difference, someone who knows how to write a batch job can also write a streaming job. Because of these powerful features, it's possible to convert batch code into streaming code with only a few very small adjustments, and the learning curve is made much easier for new users. So, let's take a closer look at how does Spark structured streaming work under the hood. Actually, this is where the concept of micro-batch comes into play. Dear friends, even though streaming seems continuous, Spark structured streaming usually splits the data into small pieces called micro-batches. Spark collects new data every few seconds or minutes, processes it as a small batch, and writes the result. You can think of this approach like this. In a factory, products come in one by one, but there's a conveyor belt system, right? Every 30 seconds, we can process all the products that have arrived up to that point together. With this particular methodology, Spark is able to leverage its existing batch infrastructure. Just like how we process data in batches, here we split it into pieces and process it. We use the existing batch infrastructure, maintain scalability, and also ensure fault tolerance. Dear friends, in the streaming world, the biggest fears are data loss and reprocessing the same data. The most critical questions in streaming operations are as follows. What happens if a job, in other words, a task, stops? Will the same data be processed more than once, or will some data be lost? So, dear friends, Spark structured streaming manages these risks using a mechanism called checkpointing. Yes, I just mentioned a new concept here, checkpoint. A checkpoint is where Spark stores information about how far it has read and written. This is like a bookmark in a book, friends. When you close the book and open it again, you continue from the last page you read. If there were no checkpoint, in other words, no bookmark, you might have to start reading the book from the beginning. Yeah, the logic is the same in streaming. In the world of streaming, the ideal goal is this. Every piece of data should be processed exactly once, friends, no more, no less, just once. Yes, friends, this is called exactly once guarantee, meaning the guarantee of processing exactly one time. Spark structured streaming comes very close to achieving this goal, especially when used together with reliable target systems like Delta Lake. This success becomes even stronger. This makes it suitable for enterprise-level data pipelines. In other words, Spark structured streaming processes data as securely as if it were being stored in a vault. It doesn't write the same data twice and doesn't lose any data, friends. This sense of reliability is one of the most important factors that makes Spark usable in large-scale, real-world systems. Dear friends, hello to everyone. As you know, in the previous lesson, we covered the topic of Spark Structured Streaming. In this lesson, we will continue from where we left off. So what are we going to do? Friends, we will examine the architecture of streaming. In other words, the big picture. So let's get started without wasting any time. A structured streaming pipeline generally consists of the following steps. There is a source, friends, the source. In other words, where is the data coming from? In the second step, there is processing. The processing step, how is the data being transformed? In the third step, there is the sync, which is the target output. Where is the data being written to? And in the fourth step, checkpointing. So how is continuity ensured? Dear friends, these four components are very similar to batch processing. However, there is a critical difference. This process runs continuously. Look, when I say stream, I'm going to repeat this a lot, just so it really sticks in our minds. It runs continuously. Continuously. Now, let's examine these components one by one. First, we'll start with the source, friends. Where's the data coming from? Dear friends, the source is the starting point of a streaming pipeline. In other words, it's the very first place where data enters the system. In structured streaming, this source is a system that continuously generates data. Ah, this could be a message queue, friends. It could be files that are continuously dropped into a folder, or it could be another data system. The important point here is this. The source doesn't produce data just once. It produces it continuously. Today, some data arrives, then a little while later, more data comes in, and this flow continues. When Spark reads from the source, it doesn't ask, is the data finished? It doesn't ask that. Instead, it asks, has new data arrived? That's what it asks. That's why, friends, in the streaming world, the source isn't just a data provider. It's also the point that sets the pace of the pipeline. The speed, order, and structure of the data directly affect the entire system. Now, let's look at the second step. The second step of the architecture is processing. How is the data transformed? Dear friends, the processing stage is the heart of the streaming pipeline. Here, the incoming raw data is transformed using Spark DataFrame APIs. We're gonna do it. Most of the operations you perform in batch processing can also be done here in the same way. These are valid here as well. For example, filtering, adding new columns, type conversions, join operations, and aggregation operations. You can do all of these here as well. However, there's an important difference in streaming. These operations don't just run once and finish. They run continuously. Guys, I'm gonna keep repeating the word continuously. Every time a new micro batch arrives, Spark applies the same transformations over and over again. So the code you write isn't something that runs once and finishes, guys. It continues to run indefinitely and becomes part of the ongoing stream. That's why the transformations written for streaming are not only specifically designed for the purpose of producing the correct result, but also at running stably for a long period of time. A seemingly minor error or a poor design choice can significantly impact the performance of a system that has been running uninterrupted for hours. Now, let's look at the third step of the architecture, sync. Where's the data being written? Dear friends, the sync is the final destination of the processed data. Look, the data has arrived, it's been processed, and now it's about to exit. This is where the output of the streaming pipeline appears. This could be a table, a file system, or another data platform. In batch processing, when a job is finished, the result is written and the process ends. However, in streaming, the sync needs to be designed to continuously accept incoming data. The target system should be able to receive data in small chunks and store it securely. At this point, you can think of the sync, the target, as a kind of destination. Just like water flowing down a river eventually reaches a lake or the sea, but the flow never really stops, right guys? The water keeps coming. So the sync needs to be robust enough to handle this constant flow. Now, let's look at the last part of the architecture, checkpoint. How is continuity ensured? Guys, the checkpoint is the unseen but most critical component of the structured streaming architecture. During streaming, the checkpoint basically acts as Spark's memory. Here, the system keeps track of what has been read so far and what has been written. We store this information here, guys. Let's say there's an interruption. Spark immediately checks the checkpoint. Thanks to the checkpoint, it can continue right where it left off. Guys, without this mechanism, streaming would never be reliable because every restart could either cause the data to be reprocessed from the very beginning or lead to some data being lost. You can think of checkpoints like markers left along a long journey. Let's say the journey gets interrupted. Well, it's no big deal. When you go back, you know exactly where to continue from. Now, dear friends, let's talk about why streaming is generally considered difficult. Dear friends, the difficulty of streaming isn't actually writing the code. You'll see this yourself when you write code in the practical lesson. It has a simple structure, but here, it's about managing continuity. Because schemas can change over time or there can be late arriving data. We call these late arriving data. Systems can stop or restart. Performance must be constantly monitored. That's why streaming solutions usually require more maintenance and more discipline. Now, friends, let's go somewhere. At this point, we're moving on to a very important topic. Where, you ask? ### Spark Structured Streaming – Checkpoint

Dear friends, hello to everyone. Welcome to our lesson. So far, we have ran streaming data together, transformed it, and safely wrote it to a Delta Lake table. Our code ran successfully. The tables were created, and we observed that the data was coming in incrementally. But now, we are going to answer a much more important question. During the streaming process, how does Spark know where it left off, and how can it continue from the same point if a problem occurs? Dear friends, the answer to this question lies in the checkpoint mechanism, which I'll take you through in the theory lesson. You can think of the checkpoint in its simplest form as Spark's memory. Streaming jobs, unlike batch jobs, don't just run once and finish. I've probably repeated this a hundred times. It represents a continuously flowing process over time. That's why Spark always needs to know this. Which data have I already processed and which are still waiting? My dear friends, the checkpoint is the specific location where Spark persistently stores all of this critical information. The moment we specify the checkpoint location parameter in our code, we're basically telling Spark, write everything related to this streaming job here and remember it from here when needed. Yes. At this point, we can think of a metaphor, dear friends. Let's use a metaphor. Think of the streaming process like a package distribution center. An incoming file gets packaged. The streaming job is an automated system that processes this package, and the Delta table is the warehouse where the packages are delivered. The checkpoint, on the other hand, is the official logbook kept by this center. This logbook records which packages have been received, which ones have been placed in the warehouse, and which ones are still on the way. Spark keeps this logbook in the checkpoint directory, and checks these records before every new operation. Every time a streaming job runs, Spark first goes to the checkpoint directory and asks, have I started this job before? If the checkpoint directory exists, Spark looks at the information there to understand which data was last processed successfully. If there is no checkpoint, Spark starts the streaming process from the very beginning. That's why the location of the checkpoint must be unique for each streaming job. Using the same checkpoint for two different streaming jobs is like two different distribution centers trying to write in the same logbook. This leads to serious confusion. There's a very important reflex in Spark's operating model, folks. First, take notes, then start working. When Spark starts a micro-batch, it writes to the checkpoint which data it will process in that batch. This is like a teacher taking attendance before starting an exam. In other words, Spark makes a note to itself. I'll process the data in this range. Friends, this approach is critically important to prevent data loss in unexpected error scenarios. Now, let's consider an even more critical scenario. The streaming job is running, data is being processed, and right at that moment, the system stops or the job fails. When Spark comes back up, it checks the checkpoint, folks. If Spark sees a record in the checkpoint indicating that the previous operation was completed, it continues with the next data. However, if it only sees a record that the operation was started and there is no record of completion, Spark will reprocess that data. At first glance, this behavior might seem risky. But in fact, this is exactly what forms the foundation of reliability in streaming. For Spark, the worst-case scenario is not processing the data at all. If necessary, reprocessing the data is always safer. This is where the importance of working with Delta Lake becomes clear. Dear friends, you can think of Delta Lake as a smart attendant in a warehouse. If the same package arrives twice, it recognizes the duplicate and keeps the process running smoothly without any disruption. So even if Spark processes the same data again, Delta Lake prevents the table from being corrupted or from creating uncontrolled duplicates. This high level of compatibility makes Spark-structured streamings exactly once guarantee, both practically applicable in real-world scenarios and consistently achievable for developers. Friends, it's also important to remind you of this in this lesson. We worked in the free edition environment and added the data manually. We ran the streaming with the available now trigger. This tells Spark, process everything that has come in so far, then stop. However, this approach doesn't change the logic of streaming. Checkpointing is still maintained. Spark still knows which data has been processed and doesn't reprocess the same files if the job is run again. So we actually simulated a real-life automatic streaming scenario in a controlled and educational way. If there were no checkpoint, Spark would have to re-read everything from the beginning every time it runs. This would mean the same data would be written over and over again, leading to incorrect results and unreliable pipelines. That's why we can say this very clearly, without a checkpoint, streaming is not acceptable in a production environment. The checkpoint is the most important aspect of Spark-structured streamings reliability and plays an indispensable role in large-scale data projects. Dear friends, now we've understood the theory, let's move on to practice. I'm opening the folder and subfolders where we wrote the checkpoints through the catalog. As you can see, the structure we see when we look at a Spark-structured streaming checkpoint directory is not random. These directories and scenarios are created by Spark's streaming engine with a standard architecture. Whether you're working in the free edition, in a production environment, using autoloader or reading data from Kafka, the checkpoint logic does not change. Dear friends, for every streaming job, Spark creates similar core components under the checkpoint directory. However, the longer the job runs and the more micro-batches are processed, the number and content of the subfiles grow over time. All right, now let's start with the metadata folder first. Friends, this folder represents the identity and structure of the streaming query. So, Spark stores information here like what kind of streaming job am I? With which configuration am I running? Which query do I belong to? Dear friends, you can think of this as the ID card of a streaming job. Thanks to this information, when the job is restarted, Spark understands that it's the same streaming job and doesn't treat it as a brand new job starting from scratch. Yes, right here is the source folder. It represents the reading side of the streaming job. Here, depending on the source, Spark keeps track of which files or which data ranges have been read. Since, in your example, this is a file-based ingestion, Spark manages the following information in this folder. Which files have I seen before and which ones are new? Guys, in other words, the source folder is like the eyes of the streaming process. It records what Spark detects in the outside world. Let's continue. Look, there's an offsets folder. It's one of the most critical parts of the streaming checkpoint structure. Before each micro-batch starts, Spark writes a record here like this. In this batch, I will process the data from this point to that point. Since this record is written before the batch actually starts, it acts like a preliminary note. Even if Spark hasn't written any data yet, it leaves this message in the offsets folder. These are the records I'm targeting. So, if the job stops halfway, Spark knows which data was planned to be processed. Look, we have a folder called commits. This complements the offsets. When a micro-batch completes, Spark writes a record to the commits folder. This record means this batch was processed successfully and the results were written to the target. Guys, when Spark restarts, it reads both the offsets and commits folders together to make a decision. If there is an offsets record for a batch but no commit record, it means this batch was interrupted and will be processed again. If both records exist, Spark safely continues with the next data. In summary, these folders in the checkpoint directory make up Spark's memory layer. Metadata represents the identity of the job. Sources represent the reading side. Offsets represent the planned work. Commits represent the work that has been successfully completed. Guys, this structure is always created with the same logic. The only thing that changes is the number of files inside. The longer the streaming job runs and the more micro-batches it produces, the richer these folders become. So, when you look at the checkpoint directory, you can actually see what Spark is thinking, what it's planning, and what it has successfully completed. That's why this directory is the physical proof of the reliability of structured streaming. Yes. Now, I'll touch on one last thing and then I'll finish the lesson. Look, when you expand the checkpoint folder here, you see numbers like 0, 1, and so on. This demonstrates the way that Spark structured streaming marks the passage of time using numbers. Spark streaming does not process data as a single uninterrupted block, friends. Instead, it treats each incoming data as a separate micro-batch. These numbers show which micro-batch Spark has processed. For example, when we load the first dataset, Spark processes it as the first micro-batch and creates a record numbered 0 in the checkpoint directory. This is like a note Spark writes to itself. I received the first data, read it, processed it, and wrote the result. Thanks to this information, Spark doesn't have to process the same data over and over again later. When we load the second dataset, since this is new data, Spark starts a second micro-batch. This time, it creates a new record numbered 1 in the checkpoint folder. So Spark is basically saying, I finished the first batch and now I've successfully completed the second batch as well. If a third dataset had been entered, this time we would see a structure numbered 2 in the checkpoint folder. The logic works exactly like this. The first incoming data is 0, the second is 1, and the third is 2. These numbers aren't random, folks. They progress in a completely sequential and deterministic way. For Spark, these numbers answer the question, how far have I progressed? Yes, the most critical point here is this. If Spark stops for any reason, if the cluster shuts down or if the job is restarted, it looks at the checkpoint folder and says, the last batch I completed successfully was batch number 1. So don't process 0 and 1 again, continue from 2. So these 0, 1, 2 structures under the checkpoint directory are Spark's memory, insurance, and roadmap. These are not the data itself, friends. They are records that show where the data processing left off. Yes, we can't open and read these files under the checkpoint folder. We can't manually examine their contents. In fact, we really shouldn't do this. These files are generated by Spark structured streaming for machines. So they're for Spark's own internal working logic. Dear friends, their contents are not in a format that humans can read. They contain binary formats, internal metadata, and Spark-specific state information. Dear friends, I think you now fully understand the topic. I tried to explain it in great detail, focusing on what you need for the exam. So I'll wrap up the Spark structured streaming topic here. In the next lesson, we'll continue with autoloader. See you in the next lesson. Take care.

## Scalable Data Ingestion with Databricks Auto Loader

### Auto Loader Fundamentals

Dear friends, hello to everyone. Welcome to our lesson. In this lesson, we will take a step into one of the most critical and in-demand topics for data engineering in the Databricks ecosystem. It's called Autoloader. Up until now, we've examined file-based streaming using Spark Structured Streaming. We watched the folders, used checkpoints, and gradually understood how the logic of streaming works, step-by-step. But here, a very natural question arises. Is this approach really sufficient for large-scale, real-world data streams? This is exactly where Autoloader comes in. It's a framework designed to answer this very question. To understand Autoloader, let's first think of it as an intelligent data ingestion system. You can compare Spark Structured Streaming to a security guard who constantly walks around a building, checking if any new data has arrived. This approach works well in relatively small-scale environments, folks. However, when there are thousands or even millions of files in a folder, this constant checking becomes both a significant cost and can cause performance issues. So, this is where Autoloader fundamentally changes the model. Now, Spark doesn't go around checking anymore. Instead, it waits for a notification. In other words, it doesn't keep asking if someone has arrived the moment someone shows up. It gets notified when someone arrives. This is exactly where the core philosophy of Autoloader comes into play. There, friends, Autoloader is a powerful system that is designed to essentially say, I will handle all of the file tracking, state management, and scalability for you, allowing you to simply focus on your data. With traditional file-based streaming, as a developer, you might have to think about a lot of details. For example, which files have been processed, which haven't, did the schema change, could duplicates occur, and so on. We can end up struggling with these kinds of questions, but Autoloader, as a layer built on top of Spark Structured Streaming, manages this complexity on our behalf. So, how does it do that? Autoloader doesn't hide the streaming engine. On the contrary, it makes it smarter and more reliable. We can also think of this with the metaphor of a smart logistic system, friends. In traditional streaming, Spark goes into the storage every time and counts all the packages one by one. We talked about this in previous lessons. Like, have I seen this before? Is this new? But with Autoloader, a sensor is placed in the storage. The system is automatically notified as soon as a new package arrives. As a result, there's no need to scan the entire storage from start to finish. This approach makes a huge difference, especially in large-scale data environments with millions of files. Because we can run into issues like listing costs or delays, things like that. These problems are significantly reduced. Another important difference with Autoloader is its scalability. In traditional streaming sources, tracking the processed files is usually handled in memory on the driver side, folks. As the data grows, this puts serious pressure on the driver. But with Autoloader, they set up this tracking on a distributed and persistent structure, as we call it. You can think of this as moving from one person keeping notes in a notebook to an enterprise-level archiving system. Yes, this way, as the data volume grows, the system will never come to you with problems like, there are too many files now. I can't keep track anymore. Yes, schema management is also another area where Autoloader really stands out. In traditional approaches, we have to define the schema from the hairy beginning, and if a new column appears in the incoming data, the job either throws an error or there's a risk of data loss. When new columns arrive, Autoloader automatically expands the schema, folks. There's also another very practical fact, my friends. Autoloader is not always the right choice. ### Auto Loader Architecture and Design Concepts

Dear friends, hello to everyone. Welcome to the class. In this lesson, we will approach autoloader not just as a feature, but as an architectural solution. In previous lessons, we examined the basic behaviors of Spark Structured Streaming. How is incremental reading done? What are checkpoints and how are they maintained? We also looked into topics like the exactly once approach and reliable writing with Delta Lake. Now, we will focus on how the autoloader, which is built on top of this engine, addresses large-scale data ingestion problems at the architectural level. So, the focus of this lesson won't be on which code we'll write, but rather on answering the question, what problems does the autoloader solve for us in the background? To understand the autoloader architecture friends, first of all, we need to grasp this fundamental truth. We need to accept this. The biggest challenge in file-based streaming is discovering and tracking files. In the classic approach, the system constantly scans the directory. It lists the files and compares them to determine which ones are new. This works on a small scale. There's no problem at all. But as the file grows friends, it starts to resemble counting all the books in a library from scratch every day. Now, the architecture of the autoloader fundamentally changes this model. It changes it from the ground up. So, how does it change it? Instead of polling, meaning constantly checking, the system is notified. The autoloader moves file discovery away from the constant scanning model to an event-driven approach. One of the key foundations of this architecture is idempotency. In other words, architecturally, the autoloader aims to guarantee this. Once a file has been processed, it will not be processed again. This isn't just a behavior, you can think of it as a design principle. The autoloader stores the identity and processing status of each file in a persistent way friends. As a result, even if the system restarts, it can confidently say, I've seen this data before. Yes, this approach solves one of the toughest problems in distributed systems at the architectural level. In other words, it eliminates the risk of reprocessing the same data. At this point, the second key component of autoloader comes into play, persistent and scalable state management. What is this? The autoloader does not keep information about processed files in temporary memory. Instead, it uses a distributed and durable state layer under the checkpoint location. You can think of this not like a single person jotting things down in a notebook, but more like an enterprise-level archiving system. As the data grows, the archive expands, but the system's behavior remains consistent. This is what makes the autoloader not just practical for small tasks, but also reliable for large-scale workloads. Friends, from an architectural perspective, the third critical concept is schema inference. When the autoloader encounters data for the first time, it doesn't just read the rows, it also tries to understand the structure of the data. This structural information is stored separately and used as a reference over time. Here's the key point, my dear friends. For the autoloader, the schema is not a fixed contract, but an entity that is tracked. In other words, the system is designed with the assumption that the data structure can change over time. This assumption is critically important for data systems in real life. Now, we're moving on to the schema evolution architecture here. With the autoloader, my dear friends, when incoming data contains something that's never been seen before, now, this is really important because this will be different from the topics I covered in previous lessons. When it detects a column that has never been seen before, it doesn't ignore it. Instead, it first records this change in the memory of the architecture. In other words, we first keep the information that the data structure has changed somewhere as a piece of information. However, the schema used by the running streaming job still remains fixed in memory. That's why when the new schema doesn't match the current schema, the system deliberately stops. Friends, you can think of this not as an error, but as a controlled stop. Autoloader leaves the decision of whether this change is intentional up to the developer. When the job is restarted, well, more precisely when it is restarted, the system continues processing with the updated schema. Yes, this is an important result of this architectural approach. Instead of silently corrupting the data, autoloader prefers to stop deliberately. This is actually a common feature of mature systems in data engineering. So the goal of the autoloader is not to keep running at all costs, but to make sure it operates correctly. When we evaluate the architecture we've discussed so far as a whole, we can clearly see this, dear friends. Autoloader brings together file discovery, reprocessing control, schema tracking, and state management under a single ingest in architecture. In other words, the Spark structured streaming engine is still running. There's no problem at all. Look, the checkpoints are still there. The micro batch model is still valid. However, autoloader adds an intelligent orchestration layer on top of this engine, making it suitable for the large scale and constantly changing world of data. In this lesson, there's another point we especially need to emphasize, a point that wasn't covered in previous explanations, friends, and that is this, autoloader does not eliminate data engineering decisions. It just makes them safer. Decisions like how to handle schema changes, whether to add new columns or where to write the data, are still architectural decisions. Autoloader reduces the impact of these decisions, but it doesn't take full responsibility for all of them. This means it's not a magical tool, but rather a mature architectural component. Dear friends, what makes autoloader powerful isn't the code we write, but the architectural perspective it offers us. One that considers data discovery, state management, and schema evolution together. That's why before using the autoloader, we need to understand how it thinks, which is what we aimed for in this lesson. Yes, I think the theory is now well understood. In the next lesson, we'll move on to more advanced topics. I'm ending the lesson here. See you soon. Take care, friends.

Because there's a registry system here that keeps a record of them. Look, number three, the line lists the offsets directory. What were offsets in the streaming world? Technically, it answered this question. Where did I leave off last? Dear friends, even though this concept is more visible in systems like Kafka, it's also file-based. In ingestion, Spark records the read boundaries and batch plans for each micro-batch here. So the offset directory acts like a log that shows which range the streaming job will target in each iteration. Yes, the fourth line. Look, it lists the commit directory. This folder is the stamp that marks the completion of the job. So after Spark successfully reads a batch and writes it to the target, it marks that this batch has been successfully completed. It writes this information under commits. That's why if there's a problem and Spark restarts, it decides what to do by comparing the offsets and commits folders. If a batch has been planned, but there's no commit, it probably got interrupted and will be reprocessed. If there is a commit, Spark can safely move on to the next step. This is what we call fault tolerance. The logic of fault tolerance comes into play exactly at this point. Yes, finally! With this line we wrote inside display, we are looking at the contents of the schema directory. This was the memory location of the schema we gave to autoloader. Autoloader extracts the schema from the first file and writes it here. Over time, if there are schema changes, the information in this directory gets updated and versioned. Yeah, since we had a schema change in the third dataset, it's especially meaningful to see the schema-related files here. This directory clearly shows us the following. Autoloader really does track the schema. Yes, friends! ## SQL-Based Data Ingestion with COPY INTO and Delta Lake

### COPY INTO Explained - A SQL-First Approach to Delta Table Ingestion

Dear friends, hello to everyone. Welcome to our lesson. In this lesson, we will learn how to load file-based data into Delta tables in the Databricks ecosystem, in a controlled, reliable, and incremental way. Yes, previously, we examined streaming and file ingestion approaches using autoloader together. Now, we will focus on understanding the logic behind the copy into command, which is especially used frequently in batch and semi-batch scenarios. By the end of this lesson, you will clearly understand the following. What problems does copy into solve? When should it be preferred? In what ways is it different from autoloader? Yes, why do we need copy into? Let's start with this question, friends. Yes, in real life, data rarely comes in ready-made tables. Data usually sits in a storage area as CSV, JSON, or Parquet files. Reading all of these files from scratch every time is both costly and risky, friends. This is exactly where copy into comes into play. Copy into is designed to take files from a specific directory and load only the necessary ones into a predefined Delta table. This way, data engineers don't have to manually track of what has been loaded and what is not. Dear friends, the philosophy of copy into is quite clear. First, the table is created, then the data is moved into this table. We can compare this to constructing a building. First, the architectural plan is drawn. The columns and floor layout are determined. Only after that are the furnishings moved inside. It's similar here. Copy into asks this right at the beginning, which column goes where? This way, schema surprises, column shifts, and unexpected data types are minimized. Especially in corporate environments, this discipline forms the foundation of data quality. My friends, one of the strongest features of copy into is its incremental loading behavior. This command automatically recognizes files that have already been processed and does not reload them. Even if you run the same command multiple times, the result doesn't change. In the world of data engineering, this behavior is called ID impotency. You can think of it like a turnstile. My friends, we've seen this in previous sessions as well. If someone passes through once, it doesn't count again if they go through a second time. Copy into also doesn't import the same file a second time. This feature provides great security, especially for scheduled plan jobs and regular batch loads. Dear friends, copy into is a SQL-centric ingestion method in the Databricks world. There's no need here to write a data frame, start a streaming query, or manage extra checkpoints. But this simplicity, friends, definitely doesn't make it weak. On the contrary, let's say it's quite powerful for certain use cases. A data engineer who knows SQL can move file-based data to Delta tables with just a few lines of code. Friends, this makes copy into especially a fast and straightforward solution for batch ETL processes. Now, let's talk about the conceptual difference between copy into and autoloader. A little bit, friends. Copy into and autoloader seem to solve the same problem, don't they? Based on what I've explained so far, it looks that way. But actually, they represent different ways of thinking. Autoloader works with continuously streaming high-volume data. It's designed for that. Copy into, on the other hand, offers a simpler approach for files that arrive at specific intervals. Yeah, autoloader is like a river. The flow never stops. Copy into, friends, is like a cargo delivery. Incoming packages are checked one by one and placed appropriately. Yeah, that's why copy into is generally used for small and medium-scale cases, let's say. Large-scale. I'm not even talking about high-scale. While it's preferred for small and medium-sized data volumes, autoloader is chosen for high-volume and continuous ingestion scenarios. It's selected, no scenarios. It's preferred. Yes, the question comes up. On which layer does copy into make more sense? That's the question. When you think about the medallion architecture, guys, the layer where copy into makes the most sense to use is the bronze layer because the purpose of the bronze layer is to bring raw data into the system in a controlled way. Copy into does exactly that, guys. It takes the files and adds them to the table without duplicating, without creating duplicates, and without causing any corruption. In the following silver and gold layers, this data is cleaned. It's enriched and analyzed. Guys, in short, copy into is a tool for discipline. Seeing copy into as just a SQL command would be incomplete. In reality, let's say data engineer, in the world of data engineering, it represents an approach that embodies the concept of controlled data ingestion. Instead of blindly accepting every incoming data set, it aims to define the rules from the very beginning and make the process repeatable. That's why, even though copy into isn't as popular as streaming, it's a quiet but reliable component in many enterprise data pipelines. I think, guys, the topic is now clear in theory. In the next lesson, we'll move on to practice and continue from where we left off. I'm ending the lesson here. See you in the next lesson. Goodbye.

## Analytics, Dashboards, and AI with Databricks SQL

### Introduction to Databricks SQL

Dear friends, hello to everyone. In the lessons we've progressed through together so far, we've used the SQL language very frequently. We've written many queries, worked with tables, analyze data, and saw SQL commands step-by-step through practical examples. But if you notice, friends, we carried out all of these activities through Databricks notebooks, that is, using the SQL cells inside the notebooks. Now we've reached an important transition point. In this lesson, we'll take SQL out of the notebooks and start treating it as a separate and independent area on the Databricks platform. In other words, we'll be exploring SQL through the Databricks SQL section available in the Databricks free edition. In this section, friends, we'll discover together what Databricks SQL is, why it's offered as a separate area, and its place in the data engineering process. But we won't approach this as if we're introducing a brand new tool. We'll treat it as a natural outcome of what we've done so far. Because now we have data that has passed through the bronze and silver layers, has been cleaned, made meaningful, and rendered reliable. So the chaos of raw data is behind us. Now it's time to make this data readable. It's time to make it interpretable and actionable for decision-making. You can think of this as a journey. The bronze and silver layers were like a long mountain hike. It was a challenging, technical, and demanding process that required attention. Databricks SQL, friends, is like the observation deck at the end of that journey, the point where we get to enjoy the view. Now we can look at the view from above and see the big picture. So what is Databricks SQL? Dear friends, Databricks SQL is not a new SQL query language developed by Databricks. The SQL used here is the standard SQL we all know. But what makes Databricks SQL important is not so much the query language itself, but the environment in which the query runs. Databricks SQL retrieves data stored in the data lake, friends, and it makes them queryable using a data warehouse logic. In other words, it allows us to run analytical queries on the existing lake house structure without moving, copying, or remodeling the data to another system. In this respect, Databricks SQL is not just a bridge between the data lake and the data warehouse, but rather a platform that combines the two. To use an analogy, friends, the data lake is like a huge warehouse. Databricks SQL, on the other hand, is like a showroom set up in front of this warehouse with organized shelves, everything labeled, and a space where customers can easily walk around. Now, I want to pause here for a moment and clarify an important point. Up to this stage, we've carried out all of our work through notebooks. We ingested the data in the bronze layer, cleaned it in the silver layer, and analyzed it in the gold layer. Naturally, this brings up the following question. If we already did everything in the notebook, was it wrong not to use Databricks SQL? The answer is no, friends. It wasn't wrong. On the contrary, this process was the right approach, both pedagogically and technically, because in data engineering, you first need to understand how the data is produced, how it is transformed, and what rules it goes through. Notebooks are the workshop for this process. In other words, it's the place where production, experimentation, and building happen. That's why we deliberately set up the bronze, silver, and gold layers through notebooks. The biggest advantage of notebooks is that they allow us to see the process step by step. In other words, it's an environment where we can instantly observe how the code works, how the data changes, and the result of every operation performed. We've seen how everything comes together. From an educational perspective, it's important to absorb these concepts. That's why, in this project, not using Databricks SQL from the very beginning was a conscious choice. So, at what points could Databricks SQL come into play? For example, if the tables we've created in the silver or gold layer have become stable and frequent, repetitive analyses will be performed on these tables, it could have been more advantageous to perform these analyses through Databricks SQL instead of using a notebook. However, since we proceeded step by step, we didn't do this in those lessons. Yes, Databricks SQL, especially when it comes to reporting, creating dashboards, and sharing with business units, Databricks SQL provides a much more suitable environment. Let's make this distinction clear. Notebooks are for data production and transformation. Guys, Databricks SQL, on the other hand, is a space where the produced data is consumed and interpreted. Up until this lesson, we focused on producing and shaping the data. Now, we're going to talk about how we can make the data we've produced more readable, more shareable, and more business-oriented. So, instead of undoing what we've done or declaring it wrong, we're moving on to the next natural step in the process. Guys, that's why you can think of the transition to Databricks SQL not as a replacement, but more like a change in rule. We're leaving the kitchen and moving into the serving area now. The data is now prepared. Now, we're going to learn how to present and explain it properly. Alright, let's continue everyone. So, why was Databricks SQL designed as a separate area? Friends, we can answer this question like this. Databricks SQL has been deliberately positioned as a separate area within Databricks. The main reason for this is to separate workloads. When data processing and data analysis use the same resources, performance and cost issues arise. Notebooks are generally used for heavy transformations, ETL processes, and batch operations. By way of contrast, Databricks SQL is specifically engineered and optimized for read-heavy, fast-response, and multi-user analytical queries. This is precisely the reason why Databricks SQL has its own unique compute structure, which is known as a SQL warehouse. Friends, you can also think of it like city traffic. What happens if trucks, passenger cars, and trams all use the same road? Traffic gets jammed. Databricks SQL eases the system by moving analytical traffic into a separate lane. Now, let's talk a bit about the logic behind SQL warehouse. Friends, in Databricks SQL, queries don't run on classic Databricks clusters. Instead, they are executed on SQL warehouses. These warehouses are specifically optimized for BI and SQL workloads. They are suitable for multiple users running queries at the same time and provide stable performance for dashboards. SQL warehouses generally come in two forms, serverless and pro-design. Serverless warehouses are managed by Databricks, and they spin up very quickly, friends. Pro-design warehouses, on the other hand, run on your own cloud infrastructure and offer more control. As a data engineer, it's more important to understand how this infrastructure works than the SQL you write here. Choosing the right warehouse, cost control, and performance optimization are your responsibilities. Alright, let's move on to another question. Who is Databricks SQL used for? Friends, Databricks SQL is not a tool designed for just one role. On the contrary, it allows different roles to come together over the same data. Analysts perform their daily analyses, business units look at dashboards, and data scientists run quick exploratory queries. And data engineers ensure that this entire structure runs smoothly. ### Using Parameters in Databricks SQL Queries

Dear friends, hello to everyone. In this lesson, we will cover a very critical topic in Databricks SQL, parameterized queries, in other words, parameterized SQL queries. Up until now, in the SQL queries we've written, we've generally used fixed values. We've written filters, conditions, and some selections directly into the query itself. Well, this approach works friends, but in real life and especially in the world of data warehousing, it's not sustainable. SQL queries written in a data warehouse are generally not one-time use friends. The same query can be run repeatedly with different values, connected to dashboards, scheduled, and processed by different users. That's exactly where SQL queries need to be dynamic. Parameterized queries friends are exactly what we need here. They provide the answers we need. Well, our goal in this lesson isn't to teach SQL. Since we are already familiar with the SQL language, our primary objective in this session is to make queries more flexible, more secure, and reusable by using the parameter mechanism that is currently provided by Databricks SQL. So instead of constantly changing the code we write, we'll learn how to control the behavior of the query from the outside. Throughout this entire lesson friends, we'll be working directly within the SQL editor, and using the real data tables found in the catalog panel. Again, by working closely with the tables in the silver OLS schema, we'll clearly see exactly how parameters are used in real-world practice. This way friends, we'll be learning the topic not with abstract examples, but through real data. Yes, by the end of this lesson, you'll have a clear understanding of this. Using parameters effectively can turn SQL queries into significantly more than just basic executable code. They make them effortlessly shareable, dashboard compatible, and fully optimized for use in professional production environments. Now, let's take a look at this transformation step-by-step together friends. So I'm opening a new query in the SQL editor. Look, I'm naming it parameterized queries. In this lesson, I'll be using the products table in particular, because this table is quite suitable for explaining parameter usage both in terms of category and column variety. Yes, first, let's clarify why we need parameters. Friends, when we write a classic query in the SQL editor, we usually write the filters directly inside the query. For example, if we want to see a specific product category, we specify this value as a constant in the query. This approach isn't a problem for one-time analyses, but when we want to run the same query again with different values, it can become a serious issue. Now, let's start with a simple example. Look, I'm pasting some code here. Yeah, we're pulling data from the products table and filtering it by product category. So for the product category name value, if it's audio, it shows up here as data for me. Let's run the code. Look, the result is here. Yes, this query works, it returns results, and at first glance, everything seems fine. There's no problem at all. But when you want to change the category value, you have to go into the query and change the code. Look, for example, I'm changing this value to automotive. I've changed it like this. All right, let's run the code. See, we got the output again, but it took some effort. At this point, well, the query becomes fragile. Especially in long and complex SQL queries, this approach is both risky and a waste of time. So this is where parameters come into play, folks. ### Scheduling SQL Queries

Dear friends, hello to everyone. In this lesson, we will cover a very critical topic on the Data BI Tech SQL side, scheduling SQL queries. In other words, we want to run certain codes automatically at specific intervals, some pieces of code. But we won't be doing this on classic fixed columns or fixed tables, but rather through a streaming scenario where data is constantly coming in. Up until now, we've seen how data coming in with autoloader is brought into the system. This data was being added to the system piece by piece at certain intervals. So the data flow is constantly ongoing. In such a situation, running queries manually is both inefficient and not a realistic approach in real life. Because as the data is constantly changing, it's not possible for us to manually intervene with the data at all times. This is where SQL scheduling comes into play. We don't stop streaming like flowing data friends, but at certain intervals on this data, we can produce meaningful results. For example, how many orders were received in the last 15 minutes? Which types of orders increased in the last hour? Or are certain metrics at the expected level? We might want to get answers to questions like these periodically. ### Inside the Query Engine – Lesson 1

Dear friends, hello to everyone. In this lesson, we're going to dive into one of the topics in Databricks SQL that most people overlook, but is actually one of the most needed in real life. We're going to try to understand how queries behave, because it's not enough for a query to just run successfully. The real question is this, how did it run, how many resources did it use, and why did it take that long? Now, up until now, since the beginning of the course, we've written SQL queries, run them, and even scheduled them. Now, our queries are running automatically. So you can think of this menu like switching between different scenes of the same movie. At the top, there's a find operator search box. And the download option lets you export the query profile. Some teams use this for performance reports, support requests, or archiving. So this screen isn't just for monitoring. It can also be used to produce evidence when needed. Now I want to tell you about a really important point. The boxes you see on this screen are a workflow lined up from top to bottom. At the very bottom, it usually starts with a scan table, so the data is read from the source. Then steps like grouping, aggregate, shuffle, sort, and window follow. In other words, the data is transformed. At the very top, you'll see a stage like result, query, or stage. That means the result is accelerated. In your workflow, you might also see a step like write into. This shows that the query is not only reading, but also performing a write operation to a table. This writing step is usually one of the most costly steps, folks. That's why, on the time graph, its bar is usually more prominent. These measurements on the right side provide us with this benefit. So instead of asking if the query is slow, we talk about where the query is slow. For example, if the shuffle step is expensive, data distribution can become an issue here. If sorting is expensive, then the need for sorting and cardinality start to be discussed. If scanning is expensive, then the amount of data read, filters, and partition pruning are talked about. So does this screen take you directly to optimization ideas? It's like a compass that leads you there. Now friends, I think this part's understood. Let's move to the left side. Look, on the left side, the first thing we see when we click on the query is the result that appears. Since I already touched on this topic before, I won't cover it here now. Right below that, there's the top operators section. This is one of the most critical panels that provides a performance summary of the query. If we think of the query profile as a movie, top operators list for us the scenes that take up the most time in this movie. In other words, the steps that consume the most time, memory, or number of rows while the query is running are highlighted here. Yes, in the top operators section, we see three different perspectives at the top. Time spent, memory peak, and rows, friends. Whichever one is selected, the list is prepared accordingly. Since time spent is currently selected, we can see what percentage of the query time is spent on which operator. This tells us the following. If the query is slow, who's to blame? Yes, for example here. For instance, you can clearly see that the writeInto operation takes up a large portion of the total time. This also tells us that the expensive part of the query is not the computation, but the writing phase. Guys, this section's especially valuable when we're talking about optimization, because now I don't think we'll be making guesses like shuffle is expensive anymore. The system directly points out to us, saying, for example, 95% of the time was spent here. So if shuffle, or sort, shows up as high here, we're questioning the need for data distribution and sorting at this point. If scanTable is high, we're talking about the amount of data being read and the filters being used. In other words, top operators is the starting point for optimization decisions. Yes, and the list right below it shows us the details of these operators one by one. On each row, you can clearly see which operator runs at each stage and how long it takes. By looking here, we can clearly say things like, this query isn't slow during computation, but rather when writing or while reading data, it's losing time. This is actually the first place senior data engineers look in real life, friends. Look, as we scroll down a bit, we see the query text section. This area shows us the executed, final, and actual SQL version of the query. In summary, while top operators answers the question of where the problem is, query text tells us in which SQL line this problem originated.
