### Building Data Connections in Databricks

Dear friends, hello to everyone. In this section, we will also discuss how we connect to data sources within the scope of Lakeflow Connect, and how we manage these connections. So far, we've seen how to bring data into the system. However, one of the most critical points in data engineering is how we access this data, and how well we design this access. In this lesson, we'll examine two approaches. First, we'll see how Databricks connects directly to cloud data using the standard connector. Then, by moving on to the managed connector structure, we will look at how we can manage these connection processes faster, more easily, and with fewer technical details. Alright friends, if you're ready, we're starting to get a deeper understanding of the connection between data sources and Databricks. Now friends, instead of thinking of the standard connector as a technical term, you can think of it as a bridge that explains how two systems communicate with each other. On one side, there's the cloud environment where the data is stored, and on the other side, there's Databricks. These two structures are independent of each other, and don't make much sense on their own. The real value emerges when we connect these two together. So, what we call the standard connector is the general name for the connection established between these two worlds. Let's think about this with an example from everyday life. You live in one city, and everything you need is in another city. If there's no road between these two cities, you can't access those resources, folks. But when a highway is built, you can go back and forth whenever you want, and meet your needs. The standard connector is exactly like this highway. It establishes a constant and reliable connection between where the data is located and Databricks. Now, depending on how you use this road, different scenarios can arise. If you go back and forth only occasionally, meaning you pull data at specific times, that's a batch approach, which we've seen in previous lessons. But if there's constant traffic, meaning data is flowing continuously, what was that, folks? That's the streaming scenario. Databricks offers you different tools for both situations. For batch, you set up simpler and more controlled connections, while on the streaming side, more dynamic and continuously running structures come into play. What matters now is how data flows, and how you manage it. Viewed differently, the standard connector is an approach, not just a tool. It answers the question, how do I connect to the data? That's the answer. Sometimes you connect to a cloud storage, sometimes to a data streaming system, and sometimes to files that are constantly being updated. But here's the common point, folks. Databricks accesses the data, reads it, and the whole process happens according to the standard connector logic. So, we've seen how Databricks connects to data in the cloud environment. In other words, how the bridge between the data and the processing engine is formed. There, we focus more on the question, how do we establish the connection? That was the main question we focused on. Now, I'm going to take this process one step further, and look for an answer to this question. Can we make this connection easier? This is where the managed connector comes into play. In data engineering, one of the most time-consuming and error-prone steps is establishing a connection to the data source. Connection details, security settings, access permissions, authentication processes, each of these requires a separate configuration. It's possible to set up this process manually. However, repeating the same steps over and over again each time is both inefficient and risky. Managed connector is an approach that simplifies this process. You can think of it like a ready-made connection panel. Instead of setting up a connection from scratch, you use a predefined structure. You just fill in the required fields. The system takes care of the remaining technical details for you. This way, you save time and establish a more secure and standardized connection. At this point, Databricks offers some connectors within itself. Look, friends, for example, Salesforce ServiceNow. See, you can connect directly to systems like SQL Server or Google Analytics from here. There are ready-made integrations available. These connectors provide quick access to frequently used data sources, especially in enterprise projects. However, in the real world, data sources are not limited to just a few systems. Companies collect data from many different platforms. At this point, Databricks works in integration with third-party solutions like Fivetran. Friends, Fivetran is a managed ETL service that can connect to hundreds of different data sources. So, by using this integration within Databricks, you can access a much broader data ecosystem. Here's the important point. The managed connector is not a standalone tool, but rather a facilitation layer. In other words, while you set up the connection yourself with the standard connector, with the managed connector, most of this process is managed automatically on your behalf. This provides a major advantage, especially when it comes to rapid development, prototyping, and building operational systems. Also, friends, this approach brings standardization to data engineering. Instead of everyone connecting in different ways, things move forward through a specific and reliable structure. This not only increases team alignment, but also makes the systems more sustainable. In summary, the standard connector answers the question, how do we establish the connection? While the managed connector answers the question, how can we do this faster, easier, and more securely? It provides the answer to that question. Yes, friends, with this, we've learned these two terms in Lakeflow Connect in every detail. I'll end the lesson here. We'll continue from where we left off in the next lesson. See you next time. Take care.

## Scalable Data Ingestion with Databricks Auto Loader

### Lakeflow Jobs - Orchestrating Data Pipelines in Databricks

Dear friends, hello to everyone. Now we're moving on to one of the most critical topics in data engineering, Lakeflow jobs. Up until now, we've seen in detail how we bring data into the system, in other words, the injection processes. Now we have data at hand. So how are we going to process this data automatically? The answer to this question is Lakeflow jobs. Yes friends, to understand this concept, we can think of it like this. You have a factory and raw materials are coming into this factory. However, raw material alone doesn't mean much. You need to process it, run it through certain stages, and finally turn it into a product. In this process, each machine does a different job. Some cut, some shape, some package. So Lakeflow jobs is the production line of this factory. You can think of each machine on this production line as a task. So pulling the data is one task, cleaning the data is another task, transforming it is another task, and finally writing it to the table is yet another separate task. Yes, these tasks don't run randomly. They proceed in a specific order, because some operations can't start until others are finished. For example, you can't clean the data before you pull it. This orderly flow is technically called a DAG, or directed acyclic graph. But instead of thinking of it as a complicated term, it's better to see it as a well-organized production line. Friends, one of the strongest aspects of Lakeflow jobs is that you don't have to write complex code to build this process. You can think of it kind of like a Lego set. We'll practice this and you'll see it clearly there anyway. You take the pieces, connect them together, and you end up with a working system. Databricks provides you with a visual interface. And through this interface, you can connect tasks to each other and build your own pipelines. This offers a huge advantage, especially in terms of rapid development and understandability. Yes, another important point is that these structures are repeatable. So once you set up a job, you can have it run automatically, every day, every hour, or based on specific triggers. This provides automation, which is one of the most important goals in data engineering. Instead of manual operations, you set up systems that run on their own. Also, this structure is not limited to just data processing. With the same logic, we can also manage the machine learning process from start to finish within this framework. You take the data, prepare it, train the model, and deploy the results. You can organize all these steps within a single job. In summary, Lakeflow jobs is where you manage the processes that make data meaningful. If the injection process is about bringing data in, then Lakeflow jobs is the mechanism that runs, processes, and generates value from that data. Alright friends, we've understood the topic theoretically. In the next lessons, we'll go through these steps one by one with hands-on practice. I'm ending the lesson here. See you in the next lesson. Take care.

## Advanced Lakeflow Jobs: Dynamic, Conditional & Data-Driven Pipelines

### Conditional Workflows in Lakeflow Jobs Lesson 1

Dear friends, hello to everyone. In this lesson, we will now move on to one of the most powerful features of Lakeflow Jobs. ### Building Dynamic Pipelines with For Each Loop Lesson 3

Dear friends, hello to everyone. In this lesson, we will learn about the for-each task within a job. Look, I'm clicking on Add task. I'm coming down to the for-each section below. I clicked on it. I'm naming the task. I'm calling it Loop Segment Task Iteration. This part is very important. Look, there's an input option. Here, I will provide the values that the loop will iterate over within the list. Because the values we enter in this field determine how many times the system will run and which values will be used in each run. Right now, there might be numbers written here as an example, but since our goal is to set up a real scenario, instead of numbers, we'll define the values of the data we want to process here. In our scenario, these values will be the customer segment information, friends. So the system will take this list as a collection and will go through each value one by one, running the same operations repeatedly. When we think about this with classic programming logic, what we're actually doing is setting up a for loop. So normally when developing software, we create a list and run the same code for each element in that list. Here, Databricks offers us the same logic visually. Look, each value we provide in the inputs field represents one iteration of the loop. The system first takes the initial value from the list and runs the relevant task with that value. Then it moves on to the second value and repeats the same process. It progresses through a process. This process continues until all the values in the list are finished. Especially, the inputs field is one of the most critical points that determines the behavior of the pipeline, folks. Because the list we provide here determines how many times the system will run, which data pieces it will work on, and therefore how many different outputs it will produce. Thanks to this, and let me repeat, this is very important, instead of writing the same business logic over and over, we can run it automatically and at scale on different data segments with a single structure. In this context, look, I'm entering the values into the list. I'm entering them as new returning in VIP. Right below that, there's another important concept, another important field, called concurrency. Look, there's an option for it. Friends, concurrency determines whether the operations inside the loop will run simultaneously or sequentially. So, the values we provide in the input section will be processed one by one, but will these operations run in parallel, or will each wait for the previous one to finish before moving on to the next? We do this by checking the concurrency setting. If we leave this value as default, the system will run the iterations sequentially. So first, the first value is processed, once that's done, then it moves on to the second, and then the third runs. This method is reliable, but especially with large data processing, it can lead to wasted time. Because, actually, we're making independent tasks wait unnecessarily. Look, I'm going to create three tables. These three tables actually have nothing to do with each other. So there's no situation where one has to finish before the other can continue. We can run all three in parallel at the same time and complete the process. In this context, when we increase the concurrency value, the system can run these iterations in parallel. For example, here we have three different segments. If we set the concurrency value to three, these three processes will start at the same time. So, the system runs the same logic in parallel for each segment. This provides significant performance and an advantage. That's why, look, I'm setting this to three here. Guys, of course, there's an important point to pay attention to here. If the operations inside the loop are dependent on each other, let me repeat, if they are dependent, if the output of one will be the input of another, then running them in parallel wouldn't be correct. But in our scenario, each segment is independent from the others, guys. That's why we did it this way. In summary, concurrency determines the speed and manner in which the operations inside the loop are executed. When used correctly, you can make your pipeline much faster and more scalable. Now, finally, I'm linking the depends on section below to the condition where the conditional task is false. Alright, now I'm going to add the task inside the loop. Look, there's a blue button at the bottom right. This button is actually one of the most critical points of the for-each structure. When you click this button, unlike adding a regular task, a special area opens inside the loop where you define the task that will run repeatedly in each iteration. Look, I'm clicking here. As you can see, it opened. So here, Databricks is telling us best, you've defined a loop, so what will run each time this loop iterates? So we answer this question with this button. That's why it's completely normal for a separate screen to open when we click it. Because now, we're stepping out of the outer pipeline and moving to a lower level where we define the logic that runs inside the loop. If we think about this in terms of classic programming, well, in the input section earlier, we actually defined a for loop. But we haven't said yet what code will be written inside the loop. When we click this button, we're actually starting to write the code block inside that for loop. So, there's a loop on the outside. And here, we're defining the operation that will run on each iteration of that loop. Now let's fill this part in. Look, I'm connecting the path to the notebook we created earlier in this job. Yes, friends, now we've come to one of the final and most critical steps, defining parameters. If you remember, we briefly touched on this topic before, just as a theory. In other words, we gave some basic information and ideas about what a parameter is and how it's used. But at that point, we didn't go into it in depth. Because at that stage, using parameters in our pipeline wasn't that critical. But now, the structure we've set up works entirely based on the logic of parameters. That's why we're going to cover this part in much more detail and with greater awareness now. Friends, the parameters field we see here is actually where we transfer a value coming from outside into the notebook. In other words, it's the bridge that allows us to use the value received in each iteration of the loop inside the notebook. A moment ago, we defined a list inside the For Each task. The system takes each value in this list one by one, in order. However, for this value to reach the notebook, we need to make a mapping here. This mapping is done exactly in this area. This part here, friends, represents the name of the variable we'll use inside the notebook. What did we do inside the notebook just a moment ago, friends? If you remember, we said dbUtilsWidgets getSegment. Do you remember? So, over on the notebook side of things, we have already defined a specific parameter called segment, and that is exactly the reason why we will write segment right here. This determines under what name the value coming from outside will be encountered inside the notebook. Dear friends, the value part indicates which value will be assigned to this parameter. And here is the most important point. We don't write this value as a constant. Look, instead of that, we use the input expression inside curly brackets. Yes, I'm clicking on the curly bracket. Look, I'm selecting the input here. My friends, this expression represents the value coming from the forEach loop at that moment. So, the system automatically fills in this field during each iteration. On the first run, no. On the second run, returning, and on the third run, the VIP value will come here and be sent to the notebook. If we think about it with a simple example, what we're actually doing here is like sending a parameter to a function. Just like how we can use the same code to produce different results by giving different values to a function, here we're also running the same code on different pieces of data by sending different segment values to the notebook. So, our code stays the same, but its behavior changes. In summary, without this parameters section, the value coming from the loop can't reach the notebook. ### Driving Pipelines with First Row Logic Lesson 1

Dear friends, hello to everyone! In this lesson, we're going to bring a new perspective to our pipeline structure. Up until now, we've mostly built structures that process all the data or work with certain parameters. ### Data-Driven Pipelines - Using SQL Tables as Dynamic Loop Inputs Lesson 1

Dear friends, hello to everyone. In our previous lessons, we built some pretty powerful and dynamic pipelines. Especially by using the lookup notebook, we managed to generate the list of tasks that the pipeline would process from within the data itself. By processing this list one by one with a for each structure, we created an automatic orchestration system. So now, the system had become not just one that processes data, but also one that determines which tasks it should work on. However, if you noticed, there was still an important point in the setup. Even though we generated the lookup list dynamically, this generation process was still happening inside a notebook. In other words, the pipeline's behavior was still technically inside the code. This, in some cases, can be limiting in terms of flexibility. For example, if we want to change the job list, we have to modify the notebook. In this lesson, we're going to take this setup one step further. Now, instead of generating the lookup data inside the notebook, we'll manage it directly through a SQL table. So the list of jobs that the pipeline will run will now be kept in the data layer independent from the code. This will give us a much more manageable and realistic structure, much closer to real-life scenarios. I especially want to emphasize this point here. The structure we'll set up in this lesson will produce the same result as the one we set up in the previous lesson. So the final output stays exactly the same. The only thing that changes is how we reach that final result. While in the previous lesson, we generated the lookup data using a notebook, from this lesson on, we'll manage the same data through an SQL table. This will show us how the same pipeline logic can be set up using different approaches. The logic behind this approach is actually quite powerful, friends, because in real projects, most of the time, which operations will run, which combinations will be processed, or which resources will be used are not defined directly in the code. So what do we give instead? These specific types of technical details, friends, are typically organized and stored in lookup tables, config tables, or metadata structures. This way, we can make the system's behavior highly adaptable and controllable through data. That's exactly what we're going to do in this lesson, friends. First, we'll create a lookup table and write the combinations that the pipeline will run into this table. Then we'll perform a read operation on this specific table with a SQL task and pass along all of the individual rows we get as input to the for each task. After that, we'll take each row, execute the processing logic with our current notebook, and finally, collect the results into a single gold table. So in short, in this lesson, we're answering these questions. How can the job list that the pipeline will run be managed independently from the code? How can SQL tables be included in the orchestration process? How can the same pipeline structure be rebuilt with different data sources? With this lesson, we'll now be able to design pipelines that are not only dynamic, yes, there's dynamism, but also centrally managed, more flexible, and much more suitable for production, friends. Within this scope, we've made our plan and schedule. We've set up our algorithm, theoretically. Now, let's see how we can put this into practice. Look, I prepared the job before the lesson. The name of the job, friends, is SQL lookup-driven delivery summary job. I gave it a name that summarizes the process like this. Look, inside the job, only our silver task is there for now. I deleted all the other tasks. Now, we're going to build our structure on top of this. Let's get started. Now, we're coming to one of the most critical steps of our pipeline. Friends, we're going to create a task, and the main purpose of this task is to generate the job list that the pipeline will run on directly on an SQL table. We won't be generating which warehouse and shipping combinations will be processed inside the notebook anymore. Instead, we'll keep this information directly in the data layer, that is, in a lookup table. This approach will give us a very important advantage because we're making the pipeline's behavior independent from the code. If we want to change which combinations will run in the future, we won't have to touch the notebook at all. We'll be able to manage the whole system just by updating this table. This is a centralized and manageable design approach that's commonly used in real-world projects. Now, let's prepare the necessary file for this task, friends. This step is critical, guys, because every time the pipeline runs, we want to generate this lookup table from scratch. So if we don't clean the table, any leftover data from previous runs could get mixed in with the new results. This would lead to incorrect or data-containing duplicate combinations. Thanks to this step, we'll have a clean list made up entirely of real combinations with no duplicates, and that's what we'll end up with, folks. So to summarize, what this task does is this. It takes meaningful and unique combinations from the silver table. It writes them neatly into a lookup table and produces a ready-to-use work list for the rest of the pipeline. So this task actually forms the foundation of the pipeline. In the next steps, we will read this table and, using a for-each structure, process each row one by one to achieve dynamic orchestration. ### Understanding DLT Building Blocks Lesson 1

Hello everyone, dear friends. In this lesson, we're moving on to one of the most critical topics of Delta Live Tables. The building blocks of DLT. If you recall, I briefly mentioned these building blocks at the end of the first DLT theory lesson. You can check the slides. So far, we've covered the general outlines of what DLT is and the pipeline logic it offers. But to truly grasp this structure, we need to understand the core components behind it one by one, friends. Because every pipeline we build in DLT is actually formed by these building blocks coming together correctly. At this point, I can say this clearly. If you use these building blocks correctly, you can easily build everything from simple to highly complex data pipelines with DLT. That's exactly what makes this approach so powerful. But if this logic isn't formed, the code you write will just be functioning pieces. It becomes harder to see the whole picture. In this lesson, we'll first focus on streaming tables, which is one of the most important building blocks. So, what is a streaming table? What does it do? What's it for? In which scenarios is it used? And how is it created in DLT? We'll understand these clearly. Then, we'll keep the theory short and go straight to practice to create our own streaming table together. If you're ready, let's start examining these core building blocks that manage DLT's real-time data flow closely. Dear friends, a streaming table is a table in DLT that reads data as a flow, or stream, and is constantly updated. In other words, data isn't read just once. As new data arrives, the pipeline automatically picks it up and updates the table. That's why this is the structure closest to real-time, friends. The logic is this. You define how you'll read the data, like with ReadStream, and DLT turns this into a continuously running table. Its most important feature is that it processes data incrementally, only on new records, not from the beginning. Now, let's move on to our work and see how we do it. Friends, we'll be working with the OLIS dataset, which we know very well. We'll work on the OrderItems dataset within this dataset. Of course, I'll also get the data from the BRAUN schema. Look, I'm starting, friends. I'm going into the Pipeline Editor. First, I said Jobs and Pipelines. Yes, I found my pipeline there. Then, I'm opening the home page by clicking Edit Pipeline. Look, it's open. Now we're familiar with this home page. Look, I'm clicking the plus icon in the middle. And I'll choose a file here. Dad, I'm clicking the Add Transformation option because this was the main place where we defined the data pipeline in DLT. In other words, the tables, transformations, and data flow we'll create are defined within these transformation files. Since we're working directly with code files rather than notebooks, the choice we make here is quite critical. ### Understanding DLT Building Blocks Lesson 3

Hello everyone, dear friends. In this lesson, we'll examine the view concept, the final building block of Delta Live Tables. In previous lessons, we ingested data with a streaming table and processed it into a permanent state using a materialized view. Now, we're moving on to views, which form the more flexible intermediate layer of the structure. Views don't store data physically, friends. They're mostly used to define transformation logic and create intermediate steps within the pipeline. So our goal here isn't to store new data. It's to make the data flow more modular, readable, and manageable. In this lesson, I'll show you what views do and how they're used in DLT in a practical way. Dear friends, what we'll do in this lesson is quite clear. Now, I want you to listen very carefully. I'm explaining the brain of the matter, the heart of it, a very important part. Look, we'll define the same operations or rather similar operations within a view. The point we need to pay special attention to here will be this. So we'll focus on making the data flow and transformation logic more modular and manageable, not on producing data. ### Enforcing Data Quality with Expectations in Delta Live Tables Lesson 1

Hello everyone, dear friends. In our previous lesson, we talked about why data quality is so important and how quality controls play such a critical role in modern data engineering projects. We also theoretically examined how the expectations mechanism within Delta Live Tables is used to meet this need. Now we're going to set the theory aside and move on to the implementation side. In this lesson, we'll create our own data quality rules and integrate these rules directly into our Delta Live Tables pipeline. From then on, it's automatic. This way, we'll have developed a structure that automatically checks whether the data coming into the system meets the standards we've said. If you recall, in previous lessons, we created various pipelines that process customer data. On these data sets, we practically developed important data engineering scenarios like AutoLoader, AutoCDC Flow, SCD Type 1, and SCD Type 2. Now, we're going to evaluate the same data flow from a different perspective. This time, our goal won't just be to move or transform the data. Instead, we'll check whether the data coming into the system is reliable or not. For example, a customer ID might come in blank, a customer name might be missing, the membership level might contain a value not defined in the system, or transaction time info might reach the system incomplete. Under normal conditions, these types of records could be included in the data pipeline and cause various problems in later layers. Not every product coming off the production line is sent directly to the customer. First, it goes through certain quality controls. While products that meet the standards continue to shipment, problematic products are separated and the necessary actions are taken. The Delta Live Table's expectations mechanism takes on a similar role in the data world. Every record coming into the system is evaluated according to the rules we've set and processed based on the result of this evaluation. We already have a working customer data flow in place. AutoLoader is monitoring this folder. The staging table receives the data, and then the AutoCDC flow processes it using SCD Type 2 logic. Now, we're going to add a quality control layer into this existing flow. So, instead of rebuilding the structure, we'll integrate data validation rules into the active pipeline. This approach is very common in real-world projects, everyone. First, the data flow is established, and then, as the system matures, data quality rules are added to it. In short, the reason we're using the same SCD Type 2 file is to show you how data quality rules are integrated into a real pipeline. The focus is on integration, so we won't be building a new architecture in this lesson. We'll add a security and quality layer to the existing architecture. So, let's get to it. Look, first, I'm adding a dictionary called customer underscore quality underscore rules at the top of the code to keep all our data quality rules in one place. I'm adding a dictionary. In this dictionary, we'll define the quality rules we want to apply to the customer data. For example, we'll say customer ID cannot be empty. We'll say customer name can't be empty. We'll say membership level can only be one of the membership levels we've specified, or we'll add rules here like operation TS cannot be empty, things like that. Now, let's add these rules. To do this, I'm pasting the code directly here, as you can see. You see the dictionary structure, right, everyone? Look, the structure we've created here is actually used to centralize the data quality rules. Easy to manage, my friends. We give each rule a meaningful name. Then, we define the control condition that corresponds to that rule. This way, the system knows in advance which fields are mandatory, which values are acceptable, and which cases should be flagged as errors. The biggest advantage of this approach, everyone, is that we can manage the data quality logic from a single point. If we want to add a new rule or change an existing one later, we only need to update this central structure instead of searching through different parts of the code. That's a much cleaner approach. This increases the code's readability and makes it easier to maintain. You could actually think of this structure like a checklist. Yes, we mentioned this, right? A factory. Look, I'm repeating this so it sticks in our minds. Just as a factory's quality control team inspects every product on the line against certain criteria, Delta Live Tables evaluates every record entering the system against this list of rules. If a record passes all the rules, it continues through the data pipeline. If it fails to pass any of the rules, we'll apply the action we've defined, everyone. This way, data quality checks will be carried out in a systematic, centralized, and manageable way. Let's see what that means in practice. In other words, we don't consider a record without a customer ID to be reliable. We consider a record without a customer name to be incomplete. We treat a membership level that isn't defined in the system as incorrect data. And a record without a transaction time, you see, we view as risky for CDC logic under these rules. Now that we've created the rules, let's move forward. Let's link these rules to our staging table. So, how are we going to do this? Take a look, everyone. We have a built-in API for this purpose. Here, I'm using the DLT expect underscore all underscore underscore drop API to apply these data quality rules. And inside it, of course, look, we've written it. What will we add? We'll add the rules. The expect all or drop expression here is quite important. This structure tells DLT the following, look, check all of these rules. We're saying, if a record fails any of these rules, don't write this record to the table. That's why I apply data quality control at the staging layer, not in the final table. Because I want the erroneous data to be caught right at the very beginning. This way, problematic records are eliminated before they even reach the auto CDC flow. Everyone, that's all there is to it. It's that simple. When we look at the rest of the existing code, we see that we haven't made any major changes. The source paths remain the same. Auto loader is still monitoring the same volume folder. The staging table still reads incoming customer update files and auto CDC flow continues to manage the SCD type 2 table. So what we did in this study was add a quality control mechanism on top of the running pipeline without disrupting its operation. In summary, everyone, in our previous structure, data was coming directly to the staging table. Now the data passes through quality rules before being written to the staging table. Records that pass the rules continue to move forward within the pipeline. Records that fail to pass the rules, however, are automatically dropped. Thanks to this small change, the pipeline is no longer just a data processing structure. It transforms into a more powerful data engineering solution that checks the reliability of incoming data. ## Recent Updates in Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines

### Recent Updates in Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines

Hello everyone, dear friends. In this lesson, we won't be developing a new pipeline, we won't be creating a new data engineering scenario, and we won't be doing any application. Instead, we'll examine a recent change released for Lakeflow declarative pipelines and discuss how this change affects our current work. Before we continue, there's one key point. I want to specifically point out that this update doesn't mean the structures we've learned so far are invalid, or that we need to change our existing code. All the examples we've developed throughout the course, the AutoCDC flow structures we used, expectations rules, streaming tables, materialized views, and other components continue to work in the same way. So there's no situation like opening and reorganizing the code you've written so far, or recreating your projects from scratch. We're not afraid. Actually, you can think of this with a car example. When a vehicle manufacturer releases a new model year, the engine is the same engine, the steering wheel is the same steering wheel, and the driving logic still works with the same logic. However, the location of some buttons might change. New features can be added, or some updates that improve the user experience might arrive. We don't need to relearn how to use the vehicle. It's enough just to be aware of the newly added features. This update for Lakeflow declarative pipelines offers a similar approach. The core data engineering logic doesn't change. Pipeline design doesn't change. The AutoCDC logic doesn't change. However, some developments in the Databricks and Apache Spark ecosystem now present us with usage options and new approaches. So then, why are we including this topic in the course? There's a very practical reason for that, because friends, in the professional data engineering world, knowing only current technologies isn't enough. At the same time, you also need to follow how platforms evolve, and in which direction they develop. Also, there are certification exams you might encounter in the future, right? Like the Databricks certification exam. Well, it's quite likely you'll see these updated structures in technical documents, blog posts, or new projects. In such a case, it's important not to be surprised when you encounter a different syntax, or a new approach, and to know that it's a development added on top of your existing knowledge. Throughout this lesson, we'll theoretically examine what the new update is, why it emerged, and how it relates to the existing Lakeflow declarative pipelines structures. With that foundation in place, let's move into the technical details. Now, let's get to exactly what the update changed on the technical side. If you remember, throughout the course, we used the DLT package to develop Lakeflow declarative pipelines in all our examples. For example, when developing a pipeline, we usually saw this structure in the first lines. Import DLT. So, later on, when we wanted to create a table, we use DLT decorators. For example, at DLT.table, right? Actually, this has been the standard approach used for many years. It continues to work today as well. With the new update, Databricks has started making some Lakeflow capabilities closer to the Apache Spark ecosystem. This opens up a new way to build our pipelines. Therefore, we can now use a new structure coming from within PySpark as an alternative. For example, our codes that used to start with import DLT, now as an alternative, look, we see it on the screen. Dear friends, look, we can start with from PySpark, import pipelines as DP. There is a very important point to note here. This new structure doesn't necessarily have to replace the old one. In other words, Databricks isn't saying you can't use DLT anymore. On the contrary, it continues to support both structures. We can see this change on the table creation side as well. Before, the structure we previously used as at DLT.table can now be used like this, at DP.table. So while the logic remains the same, the namespace has changed. In addition, there's a small but important improvement on the materialized view side. Previously, when creating a materialized view, we mostly used the same decorator structure and the system interpreted how it worked in the background. In the new approach, the purpose has become clearer. For example, we can now see a descriptive definition. At DP.materialized underscore view, a data engineer reading the code here can directly understand that the created object is a materialized view. Similarly, the naming on the temporary view side has become clearer. Instead of the structure previously used as DLT.view, it now offers you a more descriptive usage as DP.temporary underscore view. Actually, most of the changes made are concentrated exactly at this point. In other words, the data engineering logic doesn't change. Auto CDC flow doesn't change. Expectations don't change. Append flow doesn't change. SCD type 1 and type 2 don't change. The only thing that changes is mostly making some import structures and decorator definitions clearer, more readable, and more compatible with the Spark ecosystem. Therefore, if you see code like you see on the screen in a technical document, a github repo, or a certification exam in the future, don't think it's a completely new technology. Let's see what that looks like in code. My friends, look. From PySpark, import pipelines as DP. This is actually one of the updated usage forms of the lake flow declarative pipeline structure we know. While the basic logic remains the same, only some definitions have been modernized and made more compatible with the Spark world. All right, everyone. What you need to do at the end of this lesson isn't to open and convert your existing DLT code. The goal of this lesson is to get to know the new approach. If tomorrow in a technical document, as I said, in a github repo, in a blog post, and in the Databricks certification exam, you see the from PySpark import pipelines as DP structure, it was so that you could understand that this is actually one of the new representatives of the lake flow declarative pipelines world you're familiar with. I think the topic has been clearly understood. I'm ending the lesson here. See you later. Goodbye.
